# DeRot blog: full text

# Breathing Exercise Apps for iPhone, Compared: What Each Does Best

URL: https://derot.org/blog/breathing-exercise-app-iphone/
Updated: 2026-11-12

Key takeaways:
- Apple's only built-in breathing exercise is Breathe, part of the free Mindfulness app on Apple Watch: 1 to 5 minute sessions at 4 to 10 breaths per minute with haptic guidance. The listing doesn't mention inhale-to-exhale ratios or holds.
- Of the apps we checked, Unwind's listing names the most quick-start options: Lock Screen and Home Screen widgets, Control Center controls and Apple Watch complications.
- Breathwrk's US App Store listing says "Designed for iPhone", doesn't mention an Apple Watch app, and requires iOS 26.0 or later.
- Awesome Breathing (free), Breathe+ and The Breathing App all list box and 4-7-8 breathing. None of the listings we checked names the physiological sigh.
- The research backs slow breathing techniques, not any specific app. A 2023 meta-analysis found a small-to-moderate effect on stress.

The best breathing exercise app for iPhone depends on how you like to breathe and what you own. Wear an Apple Watch? Apple's free Mindfulness app is built in. Unwind gives you the most ways to start fast. Awesome Breathing offers box, 4-7-8 and coherent patterns for free. The Breathing App suits resonance breathing without ads. iBreathe and Breathe+ handle detailed custom timings.

A quick note before the list: DeRot makes an app in this category. We don't rank our own app, and no app paid to be included. Every app fact below comes from that app's US App Store listing, checked November 12, 2026.

## Breathing exercise apps for iPhone at a glance

Here's the shortlist side by side. "Not stated" means the App Store listing doesn't mention a feature. It doesn't prove the feature is missing.

| App | Best for | Patterns | Apple Watch | Health logging | Quick-start surfaces | Free option | Price (as listed, checked Nov 2026) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Apple Mindfulness | Watch owners who want free and built in | Breathe at 4-10 breaths per minute | Yes, Breathe guides you on the Watch (watchOS 8+) | Mindful minutes, State of Mind | Not stated beyond the Watch app | Fully free | Free, no in-app purchases |
| iBreathe | Custom intervals with heart rate on the wrist | Custom intervals, 0.5 s steps up to 35 s | Yes, live heart rate (watchOS 10+) | Mindful minutes | Lock Screen widget | Free with ads | Remove Ads $2.99; Unlock Premium $3.99 |
| Awesome Breathing | Named patterns at no cost | 15 programs incl. box, 4-7-8, coherent; custom | Yes, eyes-free tap mode (watchOS 10+) | Mindful minutes | Not stated (plays when locked) | Fully free | Optional support purchases $0.99-$14.99 |
| Unwind | Starting fast from anywhere | 3 guided exercises named (release notes mention 15+), plus custom | Yes, with complications (watchOS 10+) | Mindful minutes, State of Mind | Lock Screen and Home Screen widgets, Control Center, complications | Free download | Pro $1.99/week, $3.99/month, $9.99/year, $24.99 lifetime |
| Breathe+ | Long, finely tuned sessions | Box, 4-7-8, custom 1-32 s phases and holds | Not stated in this listing | Mindful minutes | Not stated | Free download | $9.99/month, $29.99/year, $69.99 Unlock Everything |
| The Breathing App | Resonance breathing without ads | Resonance 5-7 per minute, box, 4-7-8, personal ratios | Not stated | Not stated | Not stated (works with screen off) | Free tier: Resonance and Kids, up to 20 min | Premium $4.99/month or $44.99/year |
| Breathwrk | A large library on iPhone | 100+ exercises incl. 4-7-8 | Not stated ("Designed for iPhone") | Mindful minutes | Not stated (offline access) | Free with in-app purchases | In-app purchases $1.99-$69.99, billing periods mostly not stated |

## How we compared iPhone breathing apps

We compared the apps only on things that matter on an iPhone, and only on what each listing actually says. These were the five criteria:

1. **Apple Watch support.** Whether there's a Watch app, whether it offers haptic or eyes-free guidance, and whether it comes built into watchOS.
2. **Health logging.** Whether the app writes [mindful minutes](/glossary/#mindful-minutes) to Apple Health, and in some cases State of Mind entries too.
3. **How fast you can start.** Lock Screen or Home Screen widgets, Control Center controls, Watch complications, and whether a session keeps playing with the screen off.
4. **Breathing patterns.** Which patterns the listing names (box, 4-7-8, resonance or coherent) and how finely you can set custom timings.
5. **Price as listed.** Free tiers, subscriptions and one-time purchases, with billing periods where the listing gives them.

All facts come from US App Store listings checked November 12, 2026. Prices and features change, so check the listing before you pay.

We left two things out on purpose. The first is star ratings and scores. They shift week to week and say little about whether you'll open the app when your jaw is tight, and we didn't run any long-term tests that would justify a score of our own. The second is Shortcuts and Siri. None of the listings we checked mention support for either. After you install an app, open the Shortcuts app and search for the app's name. If actions show up, you can start a session from an automation, from Back Tap, or from the Action button on iPhones that have one.

## Does iPhone have a built-in breathing app?

Apple's built-in breathing exercise is Breathe, which lives inside the free Mindfulness app on Apple Watch. According to [Apple's App Store listing for Mindfulness](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/mindfulness/id1560383515), Breathe offers 1 to 5 minute sessions at 4 to 10 breaths per minute with haptic guidance. It sends reminders, logs mindful minutes to Health and Fitness, and needs watchOS 8 or later. There are no in-app purchases.

Without a Watch, you have less to work with. Apple's listing describes Breathe's guidance on Apple Watch and doesn't mention a guided breathing timer on the iPhone alone. If you don't wear a Watch, use one of the third-party apps below or a [free browser breathing timer](/tools/), which needs no install at all.

Breathe's strength is simplicity. The haptic taps let you follow along with your eyes shut, and it's already on your wrist. What it doesn't do is shape the breath. You choose a pace and a length, and that's it. The listing doesn't mention inhale-to-exhale ratios or holds, so you can't set up box breathing or 4-7-8. At 6 breaths per minute, Breathe matches the pace of calm 4-6 breathing (10 seconds per breath), but the listing doesn't say whether the exhale is longer than the inhale.

One small extra: Apple's older Watch guide notes that [heart rate recorded during Breathe sessions can be viewed in the Health app](https://support.apple.com/en-gw/guide/watch/apd371dfe3d7/6.0/watchos). It's interesting to look at, but it's not a diagnosis, and a reading from a single session doesn't tell you much.

## The apps, compared field by field

Each app gets the same five fields in the same order, so you can compare them line by line. Prices are as listed on the US App Store, checked November 2026.

### Apple Mindfulness (Breathe)

- **Best for:** Apple Watch owners who want something free and already installed.
- **How it works:** You pick a session length (1 to 5 minutes) and a pace (4 to 10 breaths per minute), then follow the animation and the haptic taps on your wrist, according to [Apple's listing](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/mindfulness/id1560383515).
- **What stands out:** There's no setup and no subscription. Mindful minutes go straight to Health and Fitness, and the app also logs State of Mind.
- **Drawbacks:** The listing describes Breathe's guided sessions on Apple Watch and doesn't mention a guided breathing timer on iPhone. It also doesn't mention ratios, holds or named patterns.
- **Price:** Free, with no in-app purchases.

### iBreathe

- **Best for:** People who like to build their own timings and want to see their heart rate live on the Watch.
- **How it works:** [iBreathe's listing](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/ibreathe-deep-breathing-exercises/id1296605806) describes custom intervals you can set in 0.5-second steps up to 35 seconds, and sessions that keep running in the background. The Watch app (watchOS 10 or later) shows live heart rate, and sessions log mindful minutes.
- **What stands out:** It has a Lock Screen widget, which cuts the taps between "I'm wound up" and "I'm breathing."
- **Drawbacks:** The free version contains ads, which some people may find distracting mid-session. It requires iOS 17 or later. If data use matters to you, check the App Privacy section of the listing.
- **Price:** Free with ads. Listed in-app purchases: Remove Ads $2.99 and Unlock Premium $3.99, plus optional tips from $0.49 to $9.99.

### Awesome Breathing

- **Best for:** Named breathing patterns at no cost, and practicing on the Watch with your eyes closed.
- **How it works:** [The listing](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/awesome-breathing-pacer-timer/id1453087953) describes 15 programs, including Box 4-4-4-4, 4-7-8 and Coherent, plus custom patterns. The Watch app (watchOS 10 or later) has an eyes-free tap mode, and the iPhone app keeps playing when the phone is locked or the app is in the background. Sessions log mindful minutes.
- **What stands out:** The whole app is free, with optional support purchases. The listing also says no data is collected.
- **Drawbacks:** The listing doesn't mention widgets or Control Center controls, so starting a session means opening the app. It requires iOS 16.4 or later.
- **Price:** Free. Optional support purchases from $0.99 to $14.99.

### Unwind

- **Best for:** Starting a session from anywhere in as few taps as possible.
- **How it works:** [Unwind's listing](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/unwind-breathing-exercises/id1470613384) names three guided exercises in its description (its release notes say the app supports 15+ breathing exercises), plus custom patterns you can adjust in 0.1-second steps. There's a Watch app (watchOS 10 or later) with complications, and sessions log mindful minutes and State of Mind.
- **What stands out:** Lock Screen and Home Screen widgets, Control Center controls and Watch complications. No other listing we checked names as many ways to start a session quickly.
- **Drawbacks:** The description doesn't name box or 4-7-8, so check whether they're among the 15+ exercises or set them up with custom timings. Over a year, the weekly Pro plan costs far more than the annual one. It requires iOS 16.4 or later.
- **Price:** Free download. Pro costs $1.99/week, $3.99/month, $9.99/year or $24.99 lifetime.

### Breathe+

- **Best for:** Fine-grained custom timings and long sessions.
- **How it works:** [The Breathe+ listing](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/breathe-breathing-exercises/id1106998959) allows inhales and exhales of 1 to 32 seconds, holds of 1 to 32 seconds, and sessions from 1 to 60 minutes. Its subtitle names box and 4-7-8 breathing, and it logs mindful minutes through HealthKit.
- **What stands out:** It gives you the most room to tinker: four adjustable phases and sessions up to an hour.
- **Drawbacks:** This listing doesn't mention an Apple Watch app. A Remove Ads purchase is listed, so expect ads in the free version. Its monthly price is the highest of the subscriptions here. It requires iOS 17 or later.
- **Price:** Free download. $9.99/month, $29.99/year or $69.99 for Unlock Everything. Remove Ads is $3.99.

### The Breathing App

- **Best for:** Resonance breathing and box breathing with no ads and no account.
- **How it works:** [The listing](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/the-breathing-app-calm-daily/id1285982210) describes Box, Resonance (5 to 7 breaths per minute), 4-7-8, and personal ratios with phases of 1 to 30 seconds and holds of 0 to 90 seconds. It works with the screen off and in the background.
- **What stands out:** There are no ads and no account. The free tier includes Resonance and a Kids option, with sessions up to 20 minutes. It supports iOS 15 or later, the oldest iOS version of any app here, which helps if your iPhone is a few years old.
- **Drawbacks:** The listing doesn't mention an Apple Watch app or Health logging. Because the free tier lists only Resonance and Kids, box and 4-7-8 appear to be Premium features. The listing shows two sets of Premium prices, so check which one you're offered.
- **Price:** Free tier. Premium is $4.99/month or $44.99/year, and $3.99/month and $39.99/year are also listed. There's a 7-day trial.

### Breathwrk

- **Best for:** A large exercise library on iPhone, especially if you already pay for Peloton.
- **How it works:** [Breathwrk's US listing](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/id1481804500?l=en-us) describes 100+ exercises, including 4-7-8, along with mindful-minute logging to Apple Health and offline access.
- **What stands out:** It has the largest library of any listing here and is the only one that mentions offline access. It's free for Peloton All Access, Guide and App+ members.
- **Drawbacks:** The listing says "Designed for iPhone" and doesn't mention an Apple Watch app, even though some roundups say it has one. It requires iOS 26.0 or later, so it won't install on iPhones running older versions. Most in-app prices don't say what billing period they cover.
- **Price:** Free download, with in-app purchases from $1.99 to $69.99.

## Which app suits box breathing, 4-7-8, resonance or a longer exhale?

Start with the technique you already like, then pick an app whose listing names it. If no listing does, any app with custom timings can handle it, and our free browser timers cover every pattern below.

| Pattern | What it is | Apps whose listing names it | Free browser timer |
|---|---|---|---|
| Calm 4-6 (longer exhale) | Inhale 4 s, exhale 6 s, 6 breaths per minute | None by name; set it with custom timings in Unwind, iBreathe, Awesome Breathing, Breathe+ or The Breathing App | [Calm breathing 4-6 timer](/tools/calm-breathing-4-6/) |
| Box | Inhale 4, hold 4, exhale 4, hold 4 | Awesome Breathing, Breathe+, The Breathing App | [Box breathing timer](/tools/box-breathing-timer/) |
| 4-7-8 | Inhale 4, hold 7, exhale 8 | Awesome Breathing, Breathe+, The Breathing App, Breathwrk | [4-7-8 breathing timer](/tools/4-7-8-breathing-timer/) |
| Resonance or coherent | Slow, even breathing at about 5-7 breaths per minute | The Breathing App (Resonance), Awesome Breathing (Coherent) | [Calm breathing 4-6 timer](/tools/calm-breathing-4-6/) |
| Physiological (cyclic) sigh | Two inhales through the nose, one long exhale through the mouth | None of the listings we checked | [Physiological sigh timer](/tools/physiological-sigh/) |
| Your own ratio | Any inhale, hold and exhale you choose | Unwind, iBreathe, Awesome Breathing, Breathe+, The Breathing App | [Custom breathing timer](/tools/custom-breathing-timer/) |

**Calm 4-6** is the simplest pattern with a longer exhale: in for 4 seconds, out for 6, which works out to 6 breaths per minute. No listing names it, but it takes about ten seconds to set up in any app with custom timings. Our guide to [4-6 breathing in 60 seconds](/blog/4-6-breathing-how-to/) covers what it should feel like and the common mistakes.

**Resonance or coherent breathing** means breathing slowly and evenly at around 5 to 7 breaths per minute. Our glossary has a short definition of [resonance frequency breathing](/glossary/#resonance-frequency-breathing). The Breathing App lists Resonance at that range, and Awesome Breathing lists a Coherent program. Apple's Breathe at 6 breaths per minute gets you close on pace, but you can't adjust the ratio.

**Box and 4-7-8** both include breath holds. Three apps name both patterns. If you're not sure how long to keep going, see [how long to do box breathing](/blog/how-long-to-do-box-breathing/). Holds aren't for everyone, so read the safety notes below first.

**The physiological sigh** doesn't appear in any listing we checked. Stanford Medicine describes [cyclic sighing](https://med.stanford.edu/news/insights/2023/02/cyclic-sighing-can-help-breathe-away-anxiety.html) like this: inhale through the nose, take a second short sip of air, then exhale slowly through the mouth, for about 5 minutes. A browser timer is the easiest way to pace it.

## Alternatives to the Apple Watch Breathe app and to Breathwrk

The best alternative depends on what's missing. People usually leave Apple's Breathe because they want to shape the breath, and they look past Breathwrk because they need a Watch app, a widget, or support for an older iOS version.

### Apple Watch Breathe app alternatives

If Breathe feels basic because you want ratios or holds on your wrist, three apps list a Watch companion:

- **Awesome Breathing:** an eyes-free tap mode, box, 4-7-8 and coherent programs, and the whole app is free.
- **Unwind:** complications, so you can start from your watch face, and custom timings in 0.1-second steps.
- **iBreathe:** live heart rate on the Watch and custom intervals up to 35 seconds.

All three need watchOS 10 or later. Apple's Breathe runs on watchOS 8 or later, so on an older Watch, Breathe may be your only option.

### Breathwrk alternatives

Breathwrk's listing is strong on library size and offline access. Look elsewhere if:

- **You want a Watch app:** Awesome Breathing, Unwind or iBreathe.
- **You want to start from the Lock Screen or Control Center:** Unwind (Lock Screen, Home Screen and Control Center) or iBreathe (Lock Screen).
- **Your iPhone isn't on iOS 26:** The Breathing App needs iOS 15 or later, Awesome Breathing and Unwind need iOS 16.4 or later, and iBreathe and Breathe+ need iOS 17 or later.
- **You want lots of named patterns without a subscription:** Awesome Breathing lists 15 programs, free.

### Free and ad-free options

The Breathing App's listing says it has no ads, and its free tier includes Resonance sessions up to 20 minutes. Apple Mindfulness (on Apple Watch) is free, and Awesome Breathing is free with optional support purchases; neither listing mentions ads. Our roundup of [what's actually free in breathing apps](/blog/best-free-breathing-apps/) goes further into free tiers and trials.

## Which breathing app should you pick?

Match the app to the moment you'll actually use it in, not to the longest feature list.

- If you wear an Apple Watch and want something free and simple, pick **Apple Mindfulness**.
- If you want to start a session from the Lock Screen, Home Screen, Control Center or your watch face, pick **Unwind**.
- If you want box, 4-7-8 and coherent breathing for free, with eyes-free guidance on the Watch, pick **Awesome Breathing**.
- If you practice resonance breathing and want no ads or account, pick **The Breathing App**.
- If you want live heart rate on your wrist while you breathe to your own intervals, pick **iBreathe**.
- If you want precise four-phase timings and sessions up to an hour, pick **Breathe+**.
- If you have a Peloton membership or want a large library that works offline, and your iPhone runs iOS 26, pick **Breathwrk**.
- If you don't want to install anything, use a [free browser timer](/tools/).

## Do breathing apps actually help, or is it just the breathing?

The research supports slow breathing techniques, not specific apps. None of the studies below tested any app in this roundup. An app's real job is to pace you and remind you. The breathing does the work.

A [2023 meta-analysis of 12 randomized controlled trials with 785 adults](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9828383/) found that breathwork reduced self-reported stress, with a small-to-moderate effect (g = -0.35). Most of the included studies had a moderate risk of bias. In the subgroup analysis, slow-paced breathing showed a significant effect and fast-paced breathing (just two studies) did not.

A [2023 remote trial](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9873947) randomized 108 people to practice for 5 minutes a day over 28 days. On the study's daily measure of positive affect (roughly, good mood), breathwork beat mindfulness meditation (+1.91 vs +1.22), and cyclic sighing did best. Heart rate variability and resting heart rate didn't change significantly, and the authors treated the work as exploratory.

On the physiology side, a [2022 review of 223 studies](https://eprints.bournemouth.ac.uk/38169/) found that voluntary slow breathing increases vagally mediated heart rate variability during sessions, right after them, and over programs with many sessions. That kind of heart rate variability is a marker linked to the "rest and digest" side of the nervous system. Put simply, slow breathing measurably changes how your body is running, at least while you're doing it and shortly after.

So what does an app add? Pacing, so you don't rush the exhale, and reminders. Both are useful. But the evidence belongs to the breathing, not to any brand, and a free timer does the same job if it's the thing you'll actually use.

## Using a breathing app in the mid-scroll moment

Knowing a technique isn't the hard part. Starting one while you're wound up is. The moment you most need a breathing app is often 20 minutes into a feed, jaw clenched and vaguely wired, which is exactly when opening another app feels like a chore. That's why quick-start options matter more than library size: a Lock Screen widget, a Control Center button or a watch-face complication can be the difference between doing it and meaning to. If the feed reliably leaves you this way, our piece on [nervous system overload from your phone](/blog/nervous-system-overload-from-phone/) explains what your body is reacting to.

A 60-second reset you can do with or without an app:

1. Put the phone face down, or lock the screen.
2. Before the first breath, let your shoulders drop and unclench your jaw.
3. Do 3 physiological sighs: inhale through the nose, take a second short sip of air, then let a long, slow exhale out through the mouth. Or do 6 rounds of in for 4 and out for 6, which takes exactly 60 seconds.
4. Notice what changed: your shoulders, your jaw, how fast your thoughts are moving.
5. Then decide on purpose: back to the feed or on to something else. Either is fine.

To be honest about the evidence: the cyclic sighing trial used 5 minutes a day. A few sighs make a shorter reset that hasn't been studied in the same way, though many people find it takes the edge off.

Friction apps take a different approach. A [PNAS field study of 280 participants](https://heibib.ub.uni-heidelberg.de/search/Record/1868867595) found that a short pause before opening an app, with the option to back out, reduced how often people opened the apps they'd targeted. (The lead author is affiliated with one sec, the app studied.) A [CHI 2024 study that followed 1,039 one sec users for about 13 weeks](https://anguilla.dbs.ifi.lmu.de/publications/hgr+24/) found that friction reduced attempts to open apps and made opening them more intentional. But users who paused the intervention quickly drifted back to their old habits. Both studies measured how often people opened apps, not how they felt after scrolling, so they don't tell us whether friction helps with the wound-up feeling itself.

## Safety notes before you start

Slow breathing with a longer exhale is low-risk for most people, and the [2022 review](https://eprints.bournemouth.ac.uk/38169/) expected few adverse effects. A few cautions still apply:

- Stop and breathe normally if you feel dizzy, lightheaded or tingly.
- Breath holds (box, 4-7-8) and fast breathing aren't for everyone. That includes pregnancy, heart or lung conditions, glaucoma, a history of seizures, and a history of fainting or panic. The [cyclic sighing trial excluded several of these groups](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9873947), so check with a clinician first.
- Never practice breath holds in or near water or while driving. Sit down when you practice.
- Some apps include fast or hyperventilation-style breathing. Be more careful with these. In the [2023 meta-analysis](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9828383/), fast-paced breathwork didn't show a significant effect on stress, and few studies reported adverse events at all.
- Heart rate in an app or in Health is for curiosity, not diagnosis.
- Breathing apps and exercises aren't a treatment for anxiety, panic or sleep problems. If distress keeps coming back, talk to a professional. If you're in crisis, call or text 988 in the US or contact your local emergency services.

## Where DeRot fits (our app)

Every app above assumes you'll remember to open it. That works well for a planned practice. It's harder when the stress comes from the feed itself: you pick up the phone to check one thing and surface 20 minutes later, shoulders up, with no memory of deciding to keep going.

DeRot pauses your apps while you reset with a few calming breaths. Instead of waiting for you to remember, it meets you mid-scroll. The breathing options are Calm (inhale 4, exhale 6, the default), Box and 4-7-8, and Pro unlocks custom routines. The aim is simple: the wired feeling fades and your head clears a little, and then you carry on or put the phone down, whichever you'd rather.

It isn't for everyone. If you want a full breathing practice with Apple Watch haptics and Health logging, the apps above do that well. If you want to be shut out of apps entirely, a hard blocker is a better fit. Our app isn't out yet. The launch newsletter on this page is the way to hear when it's ready.

## FAQ
**Which breathing apps work on Apple Watch with haptics so I can breathe with my eyes closed?**
Apple's Breathe, inside the free Mindfulness app, guides each breath with haptic taps, so you can follow along with your eyes shut. Among third-party apps, Awesome Breathing lists an eyes-free tap mode on Apple Watch. Unwind (with complications) and iBreathe (with live heart rate) also have Watch apps, but check their listings for haptic details. All three third-party Watch apps need watchOS 10 or later. Apple's needs watchOS 8.

**What is the best free breathing app for iPhone?**
It depends on what you own. If you wear an Apple Watch, Apple's Mindfulness app is free with no in-app purchases. On an iPhone alone, Awesome Breathing is free with optional support purchases and lists box, 4-7-8 and coherent patterns. The Breathing App has an ad-free free tier with Resonance sessions up to 20 minutes. iBreathe is free but shows ads unless you pay $2.99 to remove them.

**Do breathing apps save mindful minutes to Apple Health?**
Many do. According to their App Store listings, Apple Mindfulness, iBreathe, Awesome Breathing, Unwind, Breathe+ and Breathwrk all log mindful minutes to Apple Health, and Apple Mindfulness and Unwind log State of Mind too. The Breathing App's listing doesn't mention Health logging. After installing an app, make sure you allow Health access when it asks, or the minutes won't show up.

**Does Breathwrk work on Apple Watch, and why won't it install on my iPhone?**
Breathwrk's US App Store listing says "Designed for iPhone" and doesn't mention an Apple Watch app, so don't count on a Watch version. It also requires iOS 26.0 or later, so it won't install on an iPhone running an older version. If you need a Watch app on older iOS, Awesome Breathing and Unwind both list Watch apps and need iOS 16.4 or later.

**Can I add a breathing widget to my Lock Screen or Control Center?**
Yes, with some apps. Unwind's listing mentions Lock Screen and Home Screen widgets plus Control Center controls, and iBreathe's mentions a Lock Screen widget. The other listings we checked don't mention widgets. To add one, long-press the Lock Screen, tap Customize, and choose the app's widget. For Control Center, open it, tap the plus button, and add the app's control.

**How long should a breathing session be to feel a difference?**
There's no proven minimum. A 2023 trial that found mood benefits used 5 minutes a day for 28 days, and Stanford's cyclic sighing guide suggests about 5 minutes. Many people feel their shoulders drop within a minute or two of slow breathing, but that's a felt change, not a measured one. Start with 1 to 5 minutes, the range Apple's Breathe offers, and stop if you feel dizzy.

# How to De-Rot Your Brain Without Quitting Social Media

URL: https://derot.org/blog/how-to-de-rot-your-brain/
Updated: 2026-11-11

Key takeaways:
- To de-rot your brain, notice the wired feeling mid-scroll, breathe slowly with longer exhales for 30 to 60 seconds, rest your eyes on something far away, and then build a few gentler daily habits.
- Brain rot is internet slang, not a diagnosis. Oxford defines it as the "supposed deterioration" of a person's mental state, and the research on long-term effects is early and mostly correlational.
- In a 2025 meta-analysis, compulsive use (r = -.37) and emotional dependency (r = -.55) were linked with weaker cognition more strongly than time spent (r = -.20). How you scroll seems to matter more than how long.
- A strict dopamine detox is unlikely to be necessary. In a 2025 blocking trial, the benefits were partly explained by more socializing, exercise and time in nature, so adding real-world time is a gentler bet.
- The goal is to feel clear-headed after you scroll. Fewer minutes tends to follow as a side effect.

How to de-rot your brain: notice the foggy, wired feeling while you're still scrolling, breathe slowly with longer exhales for 30 to 60 seconds, rest your eyes on something far away, then build a few gentler daily habits. The goal is to come back down and feel clear-headed. Using your phone less tends to follow on its own.

None of this is a cure, and it isn't a 30-day plan. It's what to do at the moment the feed has wound you up, plus a few small changes so that moment comes around less often. You don't have to quit anything.

## Brain rot meaning: what it is, and whether it's real

Brain rot is internet slang for the foggy, slightly wired feeling after a long run of short-form video or feed scrolling. It is not a medical diagnosis and it is not literal brain damage.

When Oxford named it the 2024 word of the year, it defined brain rot as ["the supposed deterioration of a person's mental or intellectual state"](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/amp/world/brain-rot-is-oxfords-word-of-the-year), ["especially viewed as the result of overconsumption of material (now particularly online content) considered to be trivial or unchallenging."](https://www.fox6now.com/news/brain-rot-oxford-word-year-2024) Use of the term [rose 230% year on year](https://www.fox6now.com/news/brain-rot-oxford-word-year-2024). The word "supposed" is doing honest work in that definition. (We keep a shorter [definition of brain rot](/glossary/#brain-rot) in our glossary.)

In everyday use, "Reels brain rot" describes something you can feel. You close the app and a paragraph of text feels oddly heavy. Your attention skips around. You're restless without feeling rested.

### What the research actually shows

The largest look so far is a 2025 Psychological Bulletin meta-analysis of [71 studies and 98,299 participants](https://ifp.nyu.edu/2025/journal-article-abstracts/bul0000498/). Heavier short-form video use was linked with weaker attention (r = -.38) and weaker inhibitory control, which is the ability to stop yourself acting on an impulse (r = -.41). It also found a weaker overall link with mental health (r = -.21), including stress and anxiety, and no link with body image or self-esteem.

That is worth taking seriously. It is also worth reading carefully:

- Most of the studies were cross-sectional and relied on self-reported use, so [cause and effect is unclear](https://www.psypost.org/large-meta-analysis-links-tiktok-and-instagram-reels-to-poorer-cognitive-and-mental-health/). People who already struggle with anxiety or attention may reach for these apps more to cope.
- The cognition analysis rested on [14 studies, all from China](https://reason.com/2025/12/31/study-short-form-video-isnt-rotting-your-brain), and reverse causation is plausible.

So the feeling is real and common, the link is real enough to notice, and the long-term picture is early and mixed. Nobody has shown that a weekend of cat videos permanently rewires anything.

## Is it the time you spend or the way you scroll?

The way you scroll appears to matter more than the minutes. In the same meta-analysis, as [reported by Reason](https://reason.com/2025/12/31/study-short-form-video-isnt-rotting-your-brain), time spent watching was only weakly linked with cognition (r = -.20). Compulsive use, the hard-to-stop pull, was more strongly linked (r = -.37). Emotional dependency, leaning on the feed to manage how you feel, was linked most strongly of all (r = -.55). Time spent was not significantly linked with mental health (r = -.10).

These are correlations, not proof. But they match what many people notice: half an hour watching cooking videos on purpose feels different from 20 minutes of thumb-on-autopilot after a stressful email.

This is why we care about state over quantity. If a session leaves you clear-headed, the number on your screen time report matters less. Counting minutes can even backfire, because [screen time guilt tends to make the scroll worse](/blog/screen-time-guilt/), not better.

## How to de-rot your brain in the moment

The most useful place to de-rot is mid-scroll, while the wound-up feeling is actually happening. The sequence below takes about two minutes, and you can stop after any step.

### Step 1: Notice the wired feeling mid-scroll

The first step is noticing your body, because the feed's effect usually shows up physically before you put a name to it. Common cues:

- Jaw clenched, or teeth touching
- Shoulders creeping up toward your ears
- Breathing short and high in the chest, or quietly held
- Eyes fixed, face still, posture folded around the phone
- The "one more" pull: your thumb moving before you've decided to keep going

Name it without judgment. Short-form feeds are fast and endless, and a body that has been taking that in for a while tends to feel revved. That's a predictable response to the input, not a personal failing.

A five-second body check you can run anywhere: **"Jaw. Shoulders. Breath."** Unclench your jaw, drop your shoulders, and notice where your breath is sitting. If two of the three were tight, you're due a reset. For more on what's going on underneath, see our guide to [nervous system overload from your phone](/blog/nervous-system-overload-from-phone/).

### Step 2: Do a 30 to 60 second breath reset

A slow breath with an exhale longer than the inhale is one of the simplest, quickest tools most people have for bringing their body back down. Pick one of these two.

**Default: Calm 4-6 breathing (about 60 seconds)**

1. Lower the phone or set it face down.
2. Inhale gently through your nose for a count of 4.
3. Exhale slowly through your nose or softly parted lips for a count of 6.
4. Repeat for 6 rounds. That's roughly one minute at six breaths per minute.

If counting feels like one more task, follow the free [calm 4-6 breathing timer](/tools/calm-breathing-4-6/).

**Quick option: the physiological sigh (about 30 seconds)**

1. Inhale through your nose until you're comfortably full.
2. Take a short second sniff in to top up.
3. Exhale long and slow through your mouth until you're empty.
4. Do 2 or 3 rounds.

There's a free [physiological sigh timer](/tools/physiological-sigh/) if you want a guide.

**Why slow breathing helps.** A 2022 meta-analysis of 223 studies found that [slow breathing increased vagally mediated heart rate variability](https://pure.solent.ac.uk/en/publications/effects-of-voluntary-slow-breathing-on-heart-rate-and-heart-rate-/) during a session and immediately afterward. That's a marker associated with the calming, "rest and digest" side of your nervous system. In a 2023 randomized trial with 108 participants, [five minutes a day of cyclic sighing for 28 days](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9873947) raised positive mood more than mindfulness meditation and produced the biggest drop in breathing rate. The authors concluded that daily cyclic sighing [has promise as a stress management exercise](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36630953/).

To keep that honest: the trial was exploratory, participants were mostly students, the dose was five minutes a day rather than 30 seconds, and heart rate variability and resting heart rate did not change significantly in that study. Treat a one-minute reset as a way to shift how you feel right now, not as a treatment.

**What it feels like.** By the third or fourth long exhale, many people notice their shoulders settle and the urge to flick to the next video go quieter. It's subtle. You're not aiming for bliss, just a notch down.

**Common mistakes:**

- Forcing the top-up inhale on the sigh. It should be a small sip of air, not a gasp.
- Rushing the exhale. The slow exhale is the part doing the work.
- Breathing big instead of slow. Overbreathing can leave you lightheaded.
- Keeping your eyes on the feed while you breathe. Look away from the screen.

**Safety.** Stop and return to normal breathing if you feel dizzy, lightheaded or tingly. If 4-6 feels like a strain, shorten it to 3 in and 5 out. If you're pregnant, have a heart or lung condition, or have a history of fainting or panic, go gently and check with a clinician. In the 2023 trial, [about 10% of participants reported a negative experience](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9873947).

This mid-scroll moment is exactly what we built DeRot for. It meets you mid-scroll and pauses your apps while you reset with a few calming breaths, so you head back to the feed with your shoulders down and the wired feeling fading. It's coming soon to iOS. Until then, the free timers above cover the breathing.

### Step 3: Look far away and change your input

After the breath, give your eyes and attention something slow. Rest your gaze on something distant, ideally green, for about 40 seconds, then change what's coming in.

There's a small piece of evidence for the green part. In a [University of Melbourne study of 150 students](https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2015/05/150526093611.htm), those who glanced at a green roof for 40 seconds made fewer errors and responded more consistently on an attention task than those who looked at a concrete roof. The [published paper](https://findanexpert.unimelb.edu.au/scholarlywork/977781-40-second-green-roof-views-sustain-attention--the-role-of-micro-breaks-in-attention-restoration) reports fewer omission errors after the green view. It's one lab study, so keep expectations modest. Think of it as a cheap micro-break for your attention, nothing more.

No tree outside? A distant window, the sky, or the far end of the room still breaks the close, fast focus of a feed.

Then switch your input:

- Stand up and fill a glass of water.
- Step outside, even just onto a step or balcony.
- Put on one song and actually listen to all of it.
- Say something to whoever is nearby.

You don't need a speech to yourself about willpower. You're changing channel so the momentum breaks. If you go back to the app afterward, that's fine. You're going back in a different state, and that's the point.

## Do you need a dopamine detox? (Probably not)

Probably not. The strict version of a [dopamine detox](/glossary/#dopamine-detox) doesn't do what its name suggests, and gentler changes seem to capture much of the benefit.

Grinspoon, writing for Harvard Health and quoted by Mental Floss, has pointed out that [dopamine doesn't actually decrease when you avoid stimulating activities](https://www.mentalfloss.com/science/psychology/does-dopamine-fasting-actually-work). Sepah, who created dopamine fasting, recommends small, minimally disruptive experiments instead, and [extreme versions have been linked to loneliness and anxiety](https://www.mentalfloss.com/science/psychology/does-dopamine-fasting-actually-work). Skipping meals or cutting off contact with people is not a reset worth trying.

What about simply cutting the phone off? A 2025 randomized trial asked 467 adults to block mobile internet for two weeks. [91% improved on at least one outcome](https://www.news-medical.net/news/20250219/Blocking-mobile-internet-for-two-weeks-improves-mental-health-and-well-being.aspx), but only about a quarter kept the block for at least 10 of the 14 days. The gains were [partly explained by more in-person socializing, exercise and time in nature](https://usrtk.org/healthwire/blocking-mobile-phone-internet-may-boost-mood-mental-health-attention/), and the people who stuck with it had better mental health and attention to begin with.

Our read: a lot of the benefit may come from what fills the space, not from the absence of the phone. That's good news if you'd rather add real life in than go cold turkey.

## Gentler daily habits that leave you less wound up

The habits that seem most useful add calm in rather than shutting things out. Pick one or two, not all of them.

- **Add real-world time.** A walk with a friend, a workout, twenty minutes outside. These were the same things that partly explained the benefits in the [blocking trial](https://usrtk.org/healthwire/blocking-mobile-phone-internet-may-boost-mood-mental-health-attention/).
- **Watch the pull, not the clock.** Notice when "one more" turns automatic, or when you're opening the app to change how you feel. Those patterns, [more than raw time](https://reason.com/2025/12/31/study-short-form-video-isnt-rotting-your-brain), were linked with weaker focus.
- **Practice slow breathing for five minutes a day.** That was the dose in the [cyclic sighing trial](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9873947). It also makes the mid-scroll reset feel familiar when you need it.
- **Give longer attention a small, regular slot.** One chapter of a book. One full episode with no second screen. If a whole film feels hard at first, start with something shorter and build.
- **Make phone-free moments the easy default.** Charge the phone outside the bedroom, or leave it in another room during breakfast. Defaults you can break without guilt work better than rules you'll resent.

For more ways to stay connected without the comedown, see [how to stop doomscrolling without quitting your phone](/blog/how-to-stop-doomscrolling/).

You'll see pages promising your attention span back in 7 or 30 days. We haven't found good research behind those timelines. A more useful check is simple: does a scrolling session leave you clearer than it used to?

## When to talk to someone

Brain rot isn't a diagnosis, and the steps above are for everyday overstimulation. Slow breathing can help you feel calmer, but it does not treat anxiety, ADHD, depression or any other condition.

If problems with focus, mood, anxiety or sleep keep going, or start getting in the way of work, relationships or rest, talk to a doctor or mental health professional. If you're in crisis or thinking about harming yourself, call or text 988 in the US, or contact your local emergency services.

## FAQ
**Can brain rot be reversed, and how long does it take?**
The foggy, wired feeling after a long scroll usually eases once your body comes down, often within minutes of a slow-breathing reset and a change of scene. There's no good research behind the popular 7-day or 30-day recovery timelines. Most studies linking short-form video and attention are correlational, so it's unclear what, if anything, needs reversing long term. A better gauge is whether your sessions leave you clearer over time.

**Why do I feel foggy or wired after scrolling?**
Short-form feeds are fast and endless, and a body taking that in for a while often ends up tense: clenched jaw, raised shoulders, short breathing. Many people also slip into compulsive scrolling or use the feed to manage their mood, and in a 2025 meta-analysis those patterns were linked with weaker cognition more strongly than time spent. The result can feel like being restless and tired at once.

**Does TikTok or Reels actually damage your attention span?**
A 2025 meta-analysis of 71 studies found that heavier short-form video use was linked with weaker attention and inhibitory control. But most of the studies were cross-sectional and relied on self-reported use, and the cognition analysis came from 14 studies, all in China. People with existing attention struggles may simply use these apps more. So there's an association worth noticing, not proof of damage.

**How do I fix brain rot without quitting social media?**
Focus on how you feel rather than cutting minutes. Notice the wired feeling mid-scroll, do 30 to 60 seconds of slow breathing with longer exhales, look at something far away, and change your input for a minute. Over time, add more in-person time, movement and time outside, and watch for the automatic 'one more' pull. You can keep your apps and still feel clearer.

**Why can't I focus on a movie or book anymore?**
Many people notice this after a stretch of heavy short-form scrolling, and research does link compulsive short-form use with weaker attention, though cause and effect isn't clear. Stress, poor sleep and simply being out of practice can play a part too. Start small: one chapter or one episode with the phone in another room. If focus problems persist or affect daily life, talk to a professional.

**Is it the time I spend or the way I scroll?**
The way you scroll seems to matter more. In a 2025 meta-analysis, time spent was only weakly linked with cognition (r = -.20), while compulsive use (r = -.37) and emotional dependency on the feed (r = -.55) were linked much more strongly. Time spent wasn't significantly linked with mental health. These are correlations, but they suggest watching your state, not just your screen time number.

# Apps That Make You Breathe Before Opening Instagram, Compared

URL: https://derot.org/blog/app-breathe-before-opening-instagram/
Updated: 2026-11-10

Key takeaways:
- On iPhone, one sec and Clearspace show a breathing pause before Instagram opens, and ScreenZen adds a delay that can grow with each open, with breathing as one option while you wait.
- Opal's App Store listing doesn't mention breathing. It's a blocker with adjustable strictness, including a Deep Focus mode that can't be bypassed.
- Google's Pause Point is an Android feature, not an iPhone one. The closest iPhone options are third-party pause apps, Screen Time App Limits and a Shortcuts automation.
- In the 2023 PNAS study of one sec, actual app openings fell 57% over six weeks, but the study didn't measure mood or stress during or after a session.
- A pause at the open catches the reflex tap. For the wired feeling 20 minutes into a scroll, three rounds of 4-in, 6-out breathing (about 30 seconds) is a simple reset you can do anywhere.

The apps that make you breathe before opening Instagram on iPhone are one sec and Clearspace, which show a breathing pause before the app opens. ScreenZen adds a delay that can grow with each open, with breathing as an option while you wait. Opal is a stricter blocker. Apple's Screen Time and Shortcuts are free but have no breathing pause.

Disclosure: DeRot makes an app in this category. We don't rank our own app, and no app paid to be included. Every app fact below comes from that app's US App Store listing, checked November 10, 2026.

## Apps that make you breathe before opening Instagram, at a glance

| App | Best for | How the pause works | Breathing-based? | Free option | US price (as listed) | Minimum iOS |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| one sec | A breath at the open, with the choice to go in anyway | Deep-breath animation before the app opens, triggered by a Shortcuts automation | Yes | One app free | Pro $6.99/month, $19.99/year or $99.99 lifetime | iOS 15.0 |
| ScreenZen | A free pause with lots of settings | Delay before opening that can increase each time | Breathing is one option while you wait | Free (optional tips) | Tips of $5, $10, $20 or $40 | iOS 16.4 |
| Clearspace | A simple "breathe or opt out" prompt | Proceed after a deep breath or opt out | Yes | Free download (in-app purchases) | Premium from $6.99/month or $44.99/year | iOS 16.0 |
| Opal | Firm, scheduled blocking | Waiting Room with Standard or Increasing resistance; Deep Focus can't be bypassed | Not mentioned in listing | Not stated | Yearly $99.99 (plus weekly, monthly and Pro tiers) | iOS 18.0, iPhone only |
| Screen Time and Shortcuts | Paying nothing, installing nothing | App Limits on total time; an automation when an app is opened | No | Built into iOS | Free | Built into iOS |

Prices are in US dollars as shown on the US App Store, checked November 2026. "Not stated" means the listing doesn't say.

## How we compared these pause apps

We judged each app on five criteria, using only what its own App Store listing says:

1. **How it intervenes.** A delay, a breath, a message or a block.
2. **Whether breathing is built in.** Some apps are built around a breath; others are blockers that happen to have a waiting screen.
3. **How strict it is.** Can you go in anyway, and how much effort does that take?
4. **Cost.** What's free, and what the paid tiers cost per billing period.
5. **Platform.** Minimum iOS version and supported devices.

To keep the comparison even, we used only each app's App Store listing and assumed nothing beyond it. We haven't run our own long-term tests, and we don't use star ratings or review counts. Listings change, so if a price matters to you, check the App Store before you buy.

## The apps, one by one

### one sec

**Best for:** people who want a breathing animation before Instagram opens, with the choice to carry on in.

**How it works:** According to [the one sec App Store listing](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/id1532875441), the app shows a deep-breath animation before a chosen app opens, set up through an iPhone Shortcuts automation. The listing says it "delays access to distracting apps instead of blocking apps completely." After the pause, you can carry on into Instagram or close it.

**What stands out:** You get more than one kind of exercise, including box breathing and 4-7-8, and the listing also mentions options such as Follow the Dot, math and journaling. A feature called Re-Intervention sends you out of the app after a set time (the listing's example is 5 minutes) and puts you through another intervention before you can return. It's also the one app here with a peer-reviewed field study we could cite (more on that below).

**Drawbacks:** The free version covers one app, so adding TikTok or YouTube alongside Instagram means paying. Setup goes through Shortcuts, which some people find fiddly. Box and 4-7-8 both include breath holds, which aren't comfortable for everyone.

**Price:** One app free. Pro is $6.99/month, $19.99/year or $99.99 lifetime. Family is $9.99/month, $29.99/year or $149.00 lifetime (US App Store, checked November 2026). Requires iOS 15.0 or later, and the listing includes Mac.

### ScreenZen

**Best for:** people who want a free, highly adjustable pause that gets longer the more often they open Instagram.

**How it works:** [ScreenZen's listing](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/-/id1541027222) describes a delay before the app opens that can increase each time you open it, along with "Is this important" style messages. While you wait, you can do breathing or other activities.

**What stands out:** It's free, funded by optional tips. It also offers Interrupt scrolling, which the listing describes as short, limited sessions, a Practice mode, and strict blocking by time range, after a set number of opens, or through Screen Time.

**Drawbacks:** There are a lot of settings, which is either a feature or a chore depending on your temperament. Breathing is one choice during the wait rather than the core of the app. The strict mode is firmer than some people want from a speed bump.

**Price:** Free, with optional tips of $5, $10, $20 or $40 (US App Store, checked November 2026). Requires iOS 16.4 or later.

### Clearspace

**Best for:** people who want a single, simple prompt: breathe, then decide.

**How it works:** [Clearspace's listing](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/clearspace-reduce-screen-time/id1572515807?l=fr-FR) says you can "proceed after a deep breath or opt out," and frames the pause as a reminder to breathe before making decisions.

**What stands out:** The idea is plain, and the choice stays yours every time. If you don't want to tune delays or schedules, that simplicity is the point.

**Drawbacks:** The listing doesn't state how long the pause lasts, and it doesn't spell out what's free versus what needs Premium, so check before you commit.

**Price:** Free to download, with in-app purchases. Premium is listed from $6.99/month or $44.99/year, with other Premium price points ($49.99 and $59.99) shown without a billing period. Family is $79.99 (billing period not stated). US App Store, checked November 2026. Requires iOS 16.0 or later.

### Opal

**Best for:** people who want firmness: scheduled blocks and a mode that can't be bypassed.

**How it works:** [Opal's listing](https://apps.apple.com/app/opal-screen-time-for-focus/id1497465230) describes scheduled blocking, a Focus Difficulty setting, a Waiting Room with Standard or Increasing resistance, and an unblock wait you set yourself. Deep Focus is a mode that can't be bypassed or cancelled. There's also an emergency pass.

**What stands out:** You can set the strictness anywhere from a waiting room you can get through to a session you genuinely can't end early. If what you want is to be kept out of Instagram for a stretch, this is the most direct option here.

**Drawbacks:** The listing doesn't mention breathing, so it isn't really a breathing pause app. It needs a recent iOS version and runs on iPhone only. There are many pricing tiers, which takes a minute to untangle.

**Price:** Weekly $4.99 or $9.99, Monthly $19.99, Yearly $99.99, and a Pro option at $49.99 (billing period not stated). US App Store, checked November 2026. Requires iOS 18.0 or later.

### Apple Screen Time and Shortcuts (free, built in)

**Best for:** people who want to pay nothing and install nothing.

**How it works:** Screen Time App Limits set a daily allowance for Instagram. When you reach it, you see a limit screen with an "Ignore Limit" option, unless you've turned on "Block at End of Limit" ([as Apple Community users describe](https://discussions.apple.com/thread/8552371)). Separately, the Shortcuts app can run a personal automation when a chosen app ["Is Opened"](https://www.howtogeek.com/676204/how-to-automatically-launch-shortcuts-when-you-open-an-app-on-iphone-or-ipad/), so you could, for example, start a Focus when Instagram launches.

**What stands out:** It's already on your phone, and Shortcuts rewards tinkering.

**Drawbacks:** Neither includes a built-in breathing pause. App Limits kick in on total time, not at each open. A Shortcuts automation runs an action, but turning it into something that feels like a calm pause takes work.

**Price:** Free, part of iOS.

If you'd like more options in this gentle middle ground, see our comparison of [screen time apps that aren't blockers](/blog/screen-time-app-not-blocker/).

## Do pause-before-opening apps actually work? What the research shows

The best evidence comes from a 2023 PNAS study of one sec, and it shows that a short pause at the open reduces how often people go into an app. In the [field study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9974409), 719 iOS users installed the app and 280 stayed for six weeks. In 36% of attempts to open a target app, the person dismissed it after the pause. From week 1 to week 6, opening attempts fell 37% and actual openings fell 57%.

The researchers also ran an online experiment with 500 people to separate the parts of the intervention. [The option to dismiss had the strongest effect](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9974409), the time delay helped on its own but added nothing once people could dismiss, and the message on screen did not help. Put simply, what helps is a moment of friction plus an easy way out. A stern note on the screen adds little.

### What the study can't tell you

- **Self-selection.** People who installed one sec already wanted to change their habits.
- **No control group** in the field study, so some of the drop might have happened anyway.
- **Dropout.** Fewer than half of the people who started finished six weeks, which may tilt results toward people it worked for.
- **Conflict of interest.** One of the authors made the app.
- **What it measured.** Opening attempts, openings, self-reported time and satisfaction. It did not measure momentary mood or stress during or after sessions.

That last point matters for this roundup. The study supports friction at the open. It says little about how you feel once you're in the feed, or about the comedown afterward. It also shows fewer opens, not better mental health, so be cautious about any claim that a pause app makes you feel better overall.

## A pause at the open vs. how you feel 20 minutes in

A pause before opening catches the reflex tap: the thumb that lands on Instagram while the kettle boils. It does much less once you've decided to go in, which, with a pause you can dismiss, you often will. That's by design, and it's fine.

The trouble many people describe isn't the opening. It's how they feel fifteen or twenty minutes later: jaw clenched, shoulders creeping up, a vaguely wired feeling that hangs around after the phone goes down. A breath at the door doesn't reach that moment.

To be fair to the apps above, two of them do act mid-session. one sec's Re-Intervention sends you out after a set time, and ScreenZen's Interrupt scrolling keeps you to short, limited sessions. Going by their listings, though, both are about time, and their job is to end or cut short the session. They aren't designed to bring your body back down.

If that wired feeling sounds familiar, the moment you notice it is the best time for a breath, not just the open. We go deeper on what's happening in your body in [nervous system overload from your phone](/blog/nervous-system-overload-from-phone/) and [why scrolling can make you anxious](/blog/why-does-scrolling-make-me-anxious/).

## Is there Google Pause Point for iPhone?

No. Pause Point is an Android feature, not an iPhone one. [TechCrunch reports](https://techcrunch.com/2026/05/12/android-adds-a-feature-to-stop-you-from-doomscrolling/) that it's part of Android 17. It adds a 10-second pause on apps you've labelled distracting, offers breathing among other options, and requires a restart to turn off.

TechCrunch doesn't list which Android devices get it, so all we'll say is: Android, not iPhone. [one sec's own blog](https://one-sec.app/blog/pause-point-for-iphone/), which is promotional, also says it isn't available on iPhone or iPad.

On iPhone, the closest equivalents are:

- **A third-party pause app** such as one sec, ScreenZen or Clearspace, which put a breath or a delay in front of Instagram.
- **Screen Time App Limits**, if a daily cap is enough (turn on "Block at End of Limit" if you want it firm).
- **A Shortcuts "App is opened" automation**, if you'd rather build something yourself.

We don't know whether Apple will add something similar, and we won't guess.

## A 30-second Calm 4-6 breath for Instagram, before or mid-scroll

Calm 4-6 breathing is a slow breathing pattern where you inhale for a count of 4 and exhale for a count of 6, which works out to about six breaths a minute. Three rounds take about 30 seconds, and you can do it without leaving the app or installing anything.

1. Put the phone face down, or just keep your thumb still on the screen.
2. Breathe in gently through your nose for a count of 4.
3. Breathe out slowly, through your nose or softly parted lips, for a count of 6.
4. Repeat for three breaths in total, about 30 seconds.
5. On the last exhale, notice your jaw and shoulders. Let them drop if they want to.
6. Then decide: keep scrolling or close the app. Either is fine.

Use it at the open, when you catch yourself reaching for Instagram on autopilot. Or use it partway through, the moment you notice your jaw is tight or your breathing has gone shallow. If you'd like a pacer, our free [Calm 4-6 breathing timer](/tools/calm-breathing-4-6/) counts for you in the browser, and our [4-6 breathing guide](/blog/4-6-breathing-how-to/) covers the common mistakes.

### What the evidence does and doesn't say

Keep your expectations in proportion. In a [2023 Stanford randomized trial of 108 people](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/9873947/) who practiced 5 minutes a day for 28 days, exhale-focused cyclic sighing produced the largest daily gain in positive affect, and state anxiety fell in all groups. That was five minutes a day, not 30 seconds, and the findings are exploratory. A [2023 meta-analysis of 12 randomized trials with 785 adults](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9828383/) found breathwork had a small-to-moderate effect on stress (g = -0.35), with moderate risk of bias, and the authors urge cautious interpretation.

So slow breathing with a longer exhale may help you feel calmer. Thirty seconds of it won't treat anything. Think of it as a reset.

### Safety notes

- Breathe gently. Don't force big breaths.
- Stop and go back to normal breathing if you feel dizzy, lightheaded, tingly or short of breath. In the Stanford study, [about 10% of participants reported negative experiences](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/9873947/), so stopping is always fine.
- Box breathing and 4-7-8 (both offered in one sec) include breath holds. They aren't for everyone, including people who are pregnant, have heart or lung conditions, or have a history of fainting or panic.
- If anxiety, sleep problems or distress keep coming back, talk to a professional. If you're in crisis, contact local emergency services, or call or text 988 in the US.

## Which should you pick?

- If you want a breathing animation at the open with the option to go in anyway, pick **one sec** (one app free).
- If you want it free, with delays that grow each time and plenty of settings, pick **ScreenZen**.
- If you want a simple "breathe or opt out" prompt, pick **Clearspace**.
- If you want a firm block that's hard or impossible to bypass, pick **Opal**.
- If you want to pay nothing and install nothing, use **Screen Time App Limits** or a **Shortcuts automation**, knowing neither includes a breath.
- If you're on Android and want something built in, look at **Pause Point**.

And if you came looking for a mindful scroll app because opening Instagram isn't really the problem, and the feeling afterward is, the next section is for you.

## Where DeRot fits (our app)

Our app takes a different approach from everything above: it meets you mid-scroll rather than at the open. It's for people who don't mind opening Instagram but don't like how they feel twenty minutes later. DeRot pauses your apps while you reset with a few calming breaths (Calm 4-6 by default), so your shoulders can drop and the wired feeling can fade before you carry on or put the phone down.

It's coming soon to iOS and isn't available to download yet. The launch newsletter on this page is how to hear when it is.

It's not for you if you want a hard block or a gate before the app opens. In that case, one of the apps above will suit you better.

## FAQ
**Is one sec free, and how many apps does the free version cover?**
Yes, one sec has a free version, and it covers one app, according to its US App Store listing checked November 2026. To add more apps you need Pro, listed at $6.99 per month, $19.99 per year or $99.99 lifetime. A Family plan is listed at $9.99 per month, $29.99 per year or $149.00 lifetime. It requires iOS 15.0 or later.

**Can I add a pause before Instagram for free with iPhone Shortcuts or Screen Time?**
Partly. Screen Time App Limits can cap Instagram's daily time and show a limit screen, with an 'Ignore Limit' option unless 'Block at End of Limit' is on. Shortcuts can run a personal automation when Instagram 'Is Opened,' such as starting a Focus. Neither includes a built-in breathing pause, so for a breath at the open you'd need a third-party app or your own habit.

**Does one sec actually work?**
A 2023 PNAS study suggests it reduces app opens. Among 280 users who completed six weeks, actual openings fell 57% and opening attempts fell 37%, and 36% of attempts were dismissed after the pause. The study had no control group, users chose to install the app, and one author made it. It measured opens and satisfaction, not mood or stress during or after sessions.

**Which is stricter: one sec, ScreenZen, Clearspace or Opal?**
Based on their App Store listings, Opal is the strictest, with scheduled blocking, increasing resistance and a Deep Focus mode that can't be bypassed or cancelled. ScreenZen sits in the middle, with delays that grow each time and an optional strict mode. one sec says it delays access rather than blocking, and Clearspace lets you proceed after a deep breath or opt out.

**Does a pause help once I'm already deep in the feed?**
Not much. A pause at the open catches the reflex tap, but once you've chosen to go in it can't reach how you feel 15 or 20 minutes later. one sec's Re-Intervention and ScreenZen's Interrupt scrolling act mid-session, but they're time-based and nudge you out rather than calm you down. A short 4-in, 6-out breath when you notice the tension can help you feel calmer.

**Are the breathing exercises in these apps safe for everyone?**
Gentle slow breathing is generally comfortable, but stop and breathe normally if you feel dizzy, lightheaded or tingly. Box breathing and 4-7-8 include breath holds and aren't for everyone, including people who are pregnant, have heart or lung conditions, or have a history of fainting or panic. For persistent anxiety or distress, talk to a professional. In a crisis in the US, call or text 988.
