# Best Apps for Nervous System Regulation, Compared

URL: https://derot.org/blog/best-apps-nervous-system-regulation/
Updated: 2026-10-23

Key takeaways:
- The apps with the strongest backing for nervous system regulation pace slow breathing with a longer exhale or use HRV biofeedback. None of the specific apps in this roundup has published outcome trials of its own.
- A 2022 meta-analysis of 223 studies found slow breathing increased vagally mediated heart rate variability during a session, right after one, and after multi-session programs.
- Apple Mindfulness (Apple Watch) and Breathe2Relax (iPhone, iPad, Mac) are free, and they are the simplest ways to try paced breathing without a subscription.
- Most regulation apps assume you will open them at a planned, calm moment, but the moment you most need a reset is often mid-scroll, after the feed has already wound you up.
- Stop any breathing exercise if you feel dizzy or tingly. Go carefully with breath holds and fast breathing, and see a professional if anxiety persists. No app treats anxiety.

The best apps for nervous system regulation are the ones that slow your breathing and lengthen your exhale. Our shortlist: Apple Mindfulness (free, Apple Watch), Breathe2Relax (free, iPhone), Breathwrk (big exercise library), HeartMath (HRV biofeedback) and Settle (a broad somatic program). If you want to start today, free browser timers work too.

A quick disclosure: DeRot makes an app in this category. We do not rank our own app, and no app paid to be included. Every price and feature below comes from that app's own App Store listing or website, checked on October 23, 2026.

## The best apps for nervous system regulation at a glance

This list is not ranked. Each app suits a different person and a different moment, so the table is organized around how each one helps you come down, not around feature counts.

| App | Best for | How it works | Free option | Price (as listed, checked Oct 23, 2026) | Platforms |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Apple Mindfulness (Breathe) | Apple Watch owners who want free and simple | Haptic-paced breathing at 4 to 10 breaths per minute, 1 to 5 minute sessions | Free app | Free | Apple Watch, watchOS 8 or later |
| Breathe2Relax | Free paced breathing without an Apple Watch | Guided diaphragmatic breathing, optional heart rate via HealthKit | Free app | Free | iPhone, iPad, Mac (M1 or later), Vision |
| Breathwrk | Variety and guided sessions | 50+ exercises built from timed inhales, exhales and holds | Limited free tier; included for some Peloton members | Pro $9.00/month or $4.08/month billed annually, 7-day trial | iOS, Android, Web |
| HeartMath | Watching your HRV respond as you breathe | HRV coherence biofeedback via phone camera or Inner Balance sensor | Free download, Premium upgrade | Premium USD 119.99 and USD 99.00, billing period not stated | iPhone, iOS 26 or later |
| Settle | A structured program mixing breathing, tapping and somatic practices | Onboarding quiz, then 70+ practices | Free download, subscription upgrade | $4.99-$9.99/week, $4.99/month, or $59.99-$119.99/year | iPhone, iPad, iOS 16.4 or later |

## How we compared nervous system regulation apps

We compared every app on the same five criteria, using facts from official App Store listings and the apps' own websites, all checked on October 23, 2026.

1. **Method.** How it helps you come down: slow paced breathing, a longer exhale, biofeedback, or a broad mix of practices.
2. **Evidence behind the method.** We looked at the research on the approach the app uses, not at the app's marketing copy.
3. **Cost.** What the free version gives you, what the paid tier costs, and the billing period whenever the listing states one.
4. **Platforms and hardware.** Whether you need an Apple Watch, a sensor, or a recent iOS version.
5. **When you would realistically use it.** Whether it depends on you remembering, on a reminder, or on a schedule.

There are no star ratings or scores out of 10 here. We did not run a structured trial of each app, and we are not going to pretend we did. Prices also change and vary by country, so check your own storefront before you subscribe.

Two things are deliberately left out. Big meditation apps include breathing content too, but we could not verify their current features and prices for this check. Vagus nerve stimulation devices are hardware, not apps, so they are outside this roundup, and you should get medical advice before using one.

## What does the research say about breathing and nervous system regulation?

Slow, paced breathing and HRV biofeedback both have real research behind them. The apps themselves mostly do not: we found no outcome trials for any app on this list. So the fairest way to judge an app is to ask whether it uses a well-studied method, and how well it helps you actually do it.

First, some vocabulary. Heart rate variability (HRV) is the small, constant variation in the time between your heartbeats. Researchers use the part linked to the vagus nerve, called vagally mediated HRV, as one window into the calming "rest and digest" branch of the nervous system.

### Slow breathing

A [2022 meta-analysis of 223 studies](https://staffprofiles.bournemouth.ac.uk/display/journal-article/368158) found slow breathing increased vagally mediated HRV during a session, right after a single session, and after multi-session programs. The authors describe slow breathing as a low-tech, low-cost technique with few adverse effects expected.

A common research pace is about six breaths per minute, which has been [studied with and without HRV biofeedback](https://eprints.bournemouth.ac.uk/38163/7/Psychophysiology%20-%202021%20-%20Laborde%20-%20Psychophysiological%20effects%20of%20slow%E2%80%90paced%20breathing%20at%20six%20cycles%20per%20minute%20with%20or.pdf). Six breaths a minute works out to a 10-second breath cycle, which is exactly the pattern of inhaling for 4 and exhaling for 6.

### HRV biofeedback

Biofeedback adds a live readout of your heart rhythm, so you can see your breathing change it. A [2017 meta-analysis of 24 studies and 484 participants](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/psychological-medicine/article/effect-of-heart-rate-variability-biofeedback-training-on-stress-and-anxiety-a-metaanalysis/A839E9C968E54774DF5C8FB186764EF0) linked HRV biofeedback training to a large reduction in self-reported stress and anxiety (Hedges' g of 0.83 compared with control groups). The authors also say more well-controlled studies are needed.

### Breathwork compared with mindfulness

A [2023 remote randomized trial of 108 adults](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/9873947/) compared 5 minutes a day of structured breathing with mindfulness meditation over 28 days. Cyclic sighing (two inhales through the nose, then a long, slow exhale through the mouth) raised daily positive affect by 1.89 points and did better than mindfulness. The breathing practices also lowered respiratory rate more than mindfulness did. HRV and resting heart rate did not change significantly. The trial was registered after the fact, relied on self-report, and had small groups, so treat it as encouraging rather than settled.

### What this means when you pick an app

An app that paces slow breathing is using a method with solid support for raising vagally mediated HRV. A biofeedback app is using a method with promising support. "Reset your vagus nerve" is a marketing frame. The research backs a narrower claim: slow breathing is linked to higher vagally mediated HRV. None of this replaces professional care.

## The apps, compared field by field

Every app below gets the same fields in the same order: Best for, How it works, What stands out, Drawbacks, Price. That way you can compare them line by line.

### Apple Mindfulness (Breathe)

**Best for:** Apple Watch owners who want a free way to slow down with no setup.

**How it works:** Breathe now lives inside the Mindfulness app on Apple Watch. Sessions [run 1 to 5 minutes, with an adjustable breath rate and haptics](https://support.apple.com/HT206999), and your heart rate during the session is saved to the Health app. The App Store listing says it paces breathing at [4 to 10 breaths per minute with haptics](https://apps.apple.com/bh/app/mindfulness/id1560383515).

**What stands out:** It is on your wrist, so you can follow the taps with your eyes closed. Six breaths a minute falls inside its range, so you can set it to the pace that shows up most in the research.

**Drawbacks:** You need an Apple Watch running watchOS 8 or later. Reminders [fire at the start or end of the day, or at custom times](https://support.apple.com/HT206999), which means they follow the clock rather than your actual state. There is not much variety beyond one paced pattern.

**Price:** Free (App Store, checked October 23, 2026).

### Breathe2Relax

**Best for:** iPhone users without an Apple Watch who want free paced breathing and no subscription.

**How it works:** The app [guides diaphragmatic breathing and can read heart rate from an Apple Watch through HealthKit](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/-/id425720246) if you have one.

**What stands out:** It is published by the Defense Health Agency, and it runs on iPhone, iPad, Mac (M1 or later) and Vision, on iOS 15 or later. You will not run into upsells.

**Drawbacks:** The listing centers on diaphragmatic breathing, so it may feel narrow if you want a library of patterns. Like most of the apps here, you have to remember to open it.

**Price:** Free (US App Store, checked October 23, 2026).

### Breathwrk

**Best for:** People who like variety, with guided sessions for different moments of the day.

**How it works:** The official site lists [50+ exercises (100+ in Pro) built from timed inhales, exhales and holds](https://www.breathwrk.com/), and its sleep practices use an elongated exhale or humming. The iPhone app [integrates with Apple Health](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/1481804500).

**What stands out:** It is the biggest dedicated breathing library in this roundup, and it runs on iOS, Android and Web. Breathwrk is [free for Peloton All Access, Guide and App+ members](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/1481804500), so check before you pay.

**Drawbacks:** The free tier is limited. Some exercises include breath holds, which do not suit everyone (see the safety section). The current App Store version needs iOS 26 or later on iPhone (macOS 26 on Mac). We found no published outcome trials of the app itself.

**Price:** Pro is [$9.00/month, or $4.08/month billed annually, with a 7-day trial](https://www.breathwrk.com/) on the official site, checked October 23, 2026. The US App Store shows in-app purchases from $1.99 to $69.99 but does not match each price to a billing period.

### HeartMath

**Best for:** People who like seeing a number respond as they breathe.

**How it works:** HeartMath is an HRV biofeedback app. It [measures HRV coherence with your phone camera or an Inner Balance sensor](https://apps.apple.com/md/app/id6446414998) and gives you feedback while you breathe.

**What stands out:** Of the sources we cite, biofeedback is the method with a meta-analysis on self-reported stress. The camera option means you can try it without buying extra hardware.

**Drawbacks:** The listing says it is not a medical device. It needs an iPhone running iOS 26 or later. The listing we checked does not say how often Premium is billed, so check your own storefront before comparing its cost with the other subscriptions. We did not check the price of the sensor.

**Price:** Free download. Premium is listed at USD 119.99 and USD 99.00, billing period not stated (App Store, Moldova storefront, checked October 23, 2026). Your storefront may show different prices.

### Settle

**Best for:** People who want a guided program that mixes breathwork, tapping and other somatic practices.

**How it works:** You take an onboarding quiz, and then you get [70+ practices including 4-7-8, box breathing, EFT tapping and polyvagal-informed exercises](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/-/id6751709642), pitched as "2 minutes a day."

**What stands out:** It has the most variety in practice types, and it is built around the nervous-system language many readers already use.

**Drawbacks:** The listing mentions research from Stanford, Harvard and UCLA without citing specific studies, so read its claims with healthy skepticism. It has many pricing tiers, and the full experience is a subscription.

**Price:** $4.99 to $9.99/week, $4.99/month, or $59.99 to $119.99/year (US App Store, checked October 23, 2026).

### Free browser timers (ours)

We built these, so they sit in their own section and are not ranked with the apps above.

**Best for:** Trying a pattern right now without downloading anything.

**How it works:** [Our free browser breathing timers](/tools/) pace you through box breathing, 4-7-8, calm 4-6, the physiological sigh, or a custom pattern.

**What stands out:** There is nothing to install. The [calm 4-6 breathing timer](/tools/calm-breathing-4-6/) runs the six-breaths-per-minute pace from the research above, and the [physiological sigh timer](/tools/physiological-sigh/) guides the cyclic sighing pattern from the 2023 trial.

**Drawbacks:** You get no heart rate and no reminders, and you still have to remember to open a tab.

**Price:** Free.

## When do you actually use a regulation app?

Most regulation apps are built for a planned moment. Apple's reminders arrive at the start or end of the day. Settle frames its program as two minutes a day. That is a fine habit if you keep it.

But the moment you most need to come down usually is not on a schedule. You pick up your phone to check one thing, and 20 minutes later you surface with a tight jaw, raised shoulders and a vague wired buzz. Nobody in that state thinks, "Time to open my breathing app." The feed keeps the thumb moving. We wrote more about [coming down from nervous system overload mid-scroll](/blog/nervous-system-overload-from-phone/).

There is some research on why timing matters. In a [six-week field study of 280 people](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9974409), the app one sec added a short pause when people opened chosen apps, and 36% of those open attempts were then dismissed. That study measured app opens, not calm, and the app's maker was involved, so take it as a hint rather than proof. Still, it suggests that a pause that shows up right when you reach for an app can change what people do next.

So ask yourself one practical question about any app on this list: will it be there in the moment you are wound up, or only when you remember it?

### A 30-second reset you can use mid-scroll

You do not need an app for this one. It uses the 4-6 pattern, which matches the six-breaths-per-minute pace from the research.

1. Notice the cue: a clenched jaw, raised shoulders, or a thumb that keeps moving after you have stopped enjoying the feed.
2. Put the phone face down, or rest it on your leg.
3. Breathe in gently through your nose for a count of 4.
4. Breathe out slowly for a count of 6, through your nose or softly through pursed lips.
5. Repeat for 3 rounds (about 30 seconds), or up to 5 if you have time.
6. Check in. If your shoulders have dropped, decide on purpose whether to keep scrolling.

What it tends to feel like: by the second or third exhale, your shoulders drop and the buzz gets quieter. The most common mistake is gulping a huge inhale. Keep the inhale easy and let the exhale do the work. If 6 counts feels long, try 3 in and 5 out. Our guide to [4-6 breathing](/blog/4-6-breathing-how-to/) covers more variations.

## Which nervous system regulation app should you pick?

Pick the app whose method and timing match how you actually live. Here is the short version.

- **If you have an Apple Watch and want free and simple,** pick Apple Mindfulness.
- **If you want free with no subscription and no Watch,** pick Breathe2Relax or a browser timer.
- **If you want variety and guided sessions,** pick Breathwrk, and check whether your Peloton membership already includes it.
- **If you want to see your HRV change as you breathe,** pick HeartMath.
- **If you want a structured program mixing breathwork, tapping and somatic practices,** try Settle, and treat its research claims with skepticism.
- **If you want a hard lockout of your phone,** an app blocker will suit you better than anything on this list.

### Looking for an Apple Watch Breathe app alternative?

If you do not have an Apple Watch, Breathe2Relax is the closest free match: guided diaphragmatic breathing with no subscription. If you want haptic-style pacing without a watch, a browser timer you can follow by eye works too. If you have outgrown Breathe and want to see your physiology, HeartMath adds biofeedback.

### Looking for a Breathwrk alternative?

If you mainly use Breathwrk for one calming pattern, a free app like Breathe2Relax, or a browser timer, may cover what you need. If you want more practice types than breathing alone, Settle is broader. If you want feedback on whether a session is working for you, HeartMath is the biofeedback option.

## Where DeRot fits (our app)

DeRot pauses your apps while you reset with a few calming breaths. Instead of waiting for you to remember a breathing app, it meets you mid-scroll, after the feed has already wound you up, and brings you back down. Calm (inhale 4, exhale 6) is the default. Box and 4-7-8 are built in, and Pro unlocks Custom patterns. The pause is always escapable by breathing through it.

It is not for everyone. If you want a hard lockout, a meditation library, or HRV readings, one of the options above will suit you better.

It is coming soon to iOS and is not available to download yet. You can join the launch newsletter on this page, and the [free browser timers](/tools/) work today.

## Are breathing apps safe for everyone?

For most people, slow breathing with a longer exhale is low-risk. Some techniques in these apps need more care, though, and no app is a substitute for medical help.

- **Stop if you feel dizzy, lightheaded or tingly,** and go back to normal breathing. Usually it means you are breathing too deeply or too fast.
- **Go carefully with breath holds and fast breathing.** These show up in some Breathwrk exercises and in the cyclic hyperventilation used in the 2023 trial. If you are pregnant, have a heart or lung condition, have a history of fainting, or experience panic attacks, check with a clinician first and stick to gentle, slow patterns.
- **Stimulation devices are outside this roundup.** Get medical advice before using any vagus nerve stimulation device.
- **Apps do not treat anxiety, panic disorder or insomnia.** They can help you feel calmer in the moment. If anxiety, low mood or sleep problems persist, talk to a doctor or therapist. If you are in crisis, contact local emergency services, or call or text 988 in the US.

## FAQ
**What is the best free app for calming your nervous system?**
If you have an Apple Watch, the free Mindfulness app (which includes Breathe) paces slow breathing with haptics at 4 to 10 breaths per minute. Without a Watch, Breathe2Relax is free on iPhone, iPad and Mac and guides diaphragmatic breathing. Free browser timers also work. Set any of them to about six breaths per minute, for example inhale 4 and exhale 6, which is the pace most common in slow-breathing research.

**What happened to the Breathe app on Apple Watch?**
Breathe still exists, but it now lives inside the Mindfulness app on Apple Watch, which needs watchOS 8 or later. Sessions run 1 to 5 minutes, you can adjust the breath rate and haptics, and your heart rate during a session is saved to the Health app. You can also set reminders for the start or end of the day, or for custom times.

**Is Breathwrk free, and is it included with Peloton?**
Breathwrk has a limited free tier. Pro is listed on its official site at $9.00 per month, or $4.08 per month billed annually, with a 7-day trial (checked October 23, 2026). The App Store listing says it is free for Peloton All Access, Guide and App+ members, so check your membership before you pay.

**Do nervous system regulation apps actually work?**
The methods many of them use have research behind them. A meta-analysis of 223 studies found slow breathing raised vagally mediated heart rate variability, and an HRV biofeedback meta-analysis found large drops in self-reported stress. What is missing is outcome trials of the specific apps. So choose an app for a well-studied method you will actually use, not for its marketing claims.

**Is HRV biofeedback worth it, and do you need a sensor?**
HRV biofeedback has encouraging evidence: a 2017 meta-analysis of 24 studies linked it to a large reduction in self-reported stress and anxiety, though the authors want more well-controlled studies. It suits people who are motivated by seeing data. You do not always need a sensor. HeartMath, for example, can measure HRV coherence with your phone camera or with its optional Inner Balance sensor.

**Can a breathing app help with anxiety or panic attacks?**
A breathing app can help you feel calmer in the moment, and slow breathing with a longer exhale is a low-risk place to start. It is not a treatment for anxiety or panic disorder. If you have panic attacks, avoid breath holds and fast breathing unless a clinician says otherwise, and talk to a professional if symptoms persist. In a crisis, call local emergency services, or 988 in the US.

# Nervous System Overload From Your Phone: How to Come Down Mid-Scroll

URL: https://derot.org/blog/nervous-system-overload-from-phone/
Updated: 2026-10-16

Key takeaways:
- Nervous system overload from your phone is a plain-language name, not a diagnosis, for the tense, wired-but-flat state that fast, emotionally charged feeds and constant alerts can leave you in.
- In a Durham lab study of 54 young adults, Instagram use lowered heart rate but raised skin conductance, and stopping pushed both up along with self-reported stress, whether or not people scored as problematic users.
- Batching notifications three times a day improved mood and lowered stress in a 237-person experiment, while turning notifications off completely raised anxiety and FOMO.
- The most useful time to step in is mid-scroll, once you notice you're wound up: drop your shoulders, unclench your jaw, widen your gaze, and take six slow breaths of 4 counts in and 6 counts out.
- Slow breathing reliably raises vagally mediated heart rate variability across 223 studies, but evidence that a longer exhale adds extra benefit is still early and mixed.

Nervous system overload from your phone is a plain-language name (not a diagnosis) for the tense, wired-but-flat state that fast, emotionally charged feeds and constant alerts can leave you in. Early research suggests scrolling keeps your body quietly aroused, and stopping can bring a spike of stress. Slow breathing (for example 4 counts in, 6 out) is one of the better-supported ways down.

In short, the problem has less to do with how many minutes you spend and more to do with the state the feed leaves you in. You can work with that state directly, in the middle of a scroll, without deleting anything or shutting yourself out.

## What is nervous system overload from your phone?

Nervous system overload from your phone describes how your body feels after a stretch of scrolling that was supposed to be relaxing: switched on and oddly drained at the same time. It isn't a medical term, and having it doesn't mean something is wrong with you.

The felt signs tend to be physical before they are mental:

- A tight jaw, or back teeth pressed together
- Shoulders creeping up toward your ears
- A buzzy head that won't settle on one thing
- A shorter fuse with the people around you
- Trouble settling into the next task, or into sleep

Your autonomic nervous system has two broad branches that work together all day. The sympathetic side revs you up for action. The parasympathetic side, which includes the vagus nerve, helps you settle and recover. Neither one is "bad," and you are never running purely on one of them.

Lots of articles say phones keep you "stuck in fight or flight." It's a tidy story, but the research is messier than that. What the evidence actually suggests is more interesting, and more useful.

It also helps to think of this as a state, not a score. Two people can spend the same 20 minutes on the same app and come away feeling completely different, depending on what they saw, how fast it moved, and what pinged in the middle. You don't need to think of yourself as having a problem to notice that some sessions leave you rattled.

## Why does "one quick check" leave you wired?

"One quick check" tends to leave you wired because a feed packs dozens of small jolts into a few minutes: rapid topic switches, constant novelty, emotionally loaded posts, and notification interruptions. None of them is a big deal on its own. They add up.

Picture a typical two minutes. A friend's holiday photo, a clip about a disaster, a joke, an argument in the comments, an ad, then a message alert that pulls you into another app. Your attention and your emotions get pulled somewhere new every few seconds, and you rarely get to finish one feeling before the next one starts.

What you're looking at matters too. In [a survey of 800 university students in Iran and the US, doomscrolling was associated with higher existential anxiety](https://researchnow.flinders.edu.au/en/publications/doomscrolling-evokes-existential-anxiety-and-fosters-pessimism-ab/). That was a cross-sectional study, so it shows a link and doesn't prove that doomscrolling causes anxiety. Still, it matches something most people already know: five minutes of bleak headlines lands differently from five minutes of dog videos.

That is why minutes alone are a blunt measure. Pace, emotional tone and interruptions all shape how you feel afterward, not just the clock. If evenings are when this hits hardest, our piece on [why doomscrolling at night leaves you wired](/blog/doomscrolling-at-night/) goes deeper on that window.

## What happens in your body while you scroll, and when you stop

A small Durham University lab study found that scrolling Instagram lowered heart rate while raising skin conductance, a common marker of arousal, and that stopping pushed both up along with stress. Put simply, you can seem absorbed and still while you scroll, then feel edgy the moment you put the phone down.

Here are the details. [Researchers had 54 young adults use Instagram for 15 minutes. Compared with a baseline reading task, heart rate went down and skin conductance went up](https://durham-repository.worktribe.com/OutputFile/3489734). Skin conductance tracks tiny changes in sweat gland activity, which is why researchers use it as a sign of physiological arousal. So the picture during scrolling wasn't panic. It was closer to absorbed and quietly switched on at the same time.

The more striking part came afterward. [When participants stopped, their heart rate and skin conductance rose, and they reported stress, anxiety and craving](https://durham-repository.worktribe.com/OutputFile/3489734). As one of the researchers described it, [skin conductance climbed further when the session was interrupted](https://www.sciencealert.com/scrolling-through-social-media-has-a-unique-effect-on-your-body).

That maps neatly onto the "wired but flat" feeling. While you scroll, you're absorbed and physically still. When you stop, there's a small surge, and you look up at your kitchen with a tight jaw and an itch to pick the phone back up.

There are two important caveats:

- **This isn't about addiction.** [The physiological pattern was not associated with participants' problematic-use scores](https://durham-repository.worktribe.com/OutputFile/3489734), so it showed up in ordinary users and not only heavy ones. The author [does not conclude that everyone is addicted, and says it is unclear whether the log-off response is withdrawal](https://www.sciencealert.com/scrolling-through-social-media-has-a-unique-effect-on-your-body).
- **It's one small study.** Fifty-four young adults, one app, in a lab. It's a useful clue, not a settled fact.

The practical point is that the moment you stop scrolling is a pressure point of its own, and a short reset there can help.

## Do notifications and fast-switching feeds make it worse?

Notifications seem to add to the load, but cutting them off completely isn't automatically better. The best available evidence favors batching alerts over silencing everything.

In [a study of 221 people, participants reported more inattention and hyperactivity during a week with phone alerts on than during a week with them off, and that inattention predicted lower well-being](https://www.interruptions.net/literature/Kushlev-CHI16.pdf). The study relied on self-report and doesn't show that phones cause ADHD. What it does suggest is that a steady trickle of pings makes it harder to feel settled.

A later field experiment adds an important twist. In [a 237-person study, getting notifications in batches three times a day improved mood and lowered stress, while getting no notifications at all raised anxiety and fear of missing out](https://scholars.duke.edu/publication/1402953). It's a single experiment, so treat it as a strong hint rather than a rule.

That second finding matters. Switching every alert off can backfire, because worrying about what you're missing turns into its own source of tension. Fewer, predictable interruptions seem to work better than none.

## Does hunching over your phone change how you breathe?

Possibly, but the evidence is thin. One small study found heavier phone users had more forward head posture and weaker forceful exhales, while other lung measures didn't differ significantly.

In [a study of 50 people, those who used a smartphone more than 4 hours a day had more forward head posture and lower peak expiratory flow, but their forced vital capacity and FEV1 did not differ significantly](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4756000/). Peak expiratory flow measures how hard you can blow out, not how you breathe at rest, so it tells us little about breathing while you scroll.

You might notice something for yourself, though: shallow, upper-chest breathing when you're hunched and absorbed, or holding your breath while you read something tense. That's worth paying attention to. Just treat it as something you observe in yourself, not an established mechanism. We're skipping the catchy labels here, because the research hasn't caught up with them.

## How to calm down when you're overstimulated mid-scroll

The best time to calm down is mid-scroll, right when you notice you're wound up, not at a gate before you open the app. That's when the overstimulated feeling is actually there. And the Durham findings suggest the comedown, when you stop, is when stress tends to rise.

A pause before you open an app catches you at a moment when you're usually fine. A mid-scroll pause catches you when you aren't.

### The 60-second script

1. **Notice and name it.** Say it in your head: "I'm wound up." Naming the state is your cue to switch, and it keeps the reset from feeling like a punishment.
2. **Drop your shoulders.** Lift them slightly toward your ears, then let them fall. Let your arms feel heavy.
3. **Unclench your jaw.** Let your back teeth part a little. Your lips can stay closed, with your tongue resting softly in your mouth.
4. **Widen your gaze.** Look up from the screen and take in the edges of the room (the walls, the window, the ceiling) without focusing hard on anything.
5. **Breathe in for 4, out for 6.** Inhale gently through your nose for a count of 4, then breathe out slowly for a count of 6. Each breath takes about 10 seconds.
6. **Repeat for six breaths.** Six breaths of 4 in and 6 out takes one minute, which works out to six breaths per minute. Then decide on purpose whether to keep scrolling.

Steps 2 to 4 take a few seconds, so fold them into your first breath or two. If you'd like a pacer, the [calm 4-6 breathing timer](/tools/calm-breathing-4-6/) counts for you, and our [guide to 4-6 breathing](/blog/4-6-breathing-how-to/) covers variations and how to adjust the counts.

### What it feels like, and common mistakes

The first two breaths usually feel a little awkward. By the fourth or fifth, many people find their shoulders have dropped further on their own and their head has gone quieter. You're not aiming for bliss. You're aiming to come down a notch.

Common mistakes:

- **Forcing the exhale.** Six counts should feel like a slow leak, not a push. If you run out of air early, count a bit faster.
- **Overfilling your lungs.** A 4-count inhale is a normal-sized breath, not a gulp.
- **Checking the feed between breaths.** One glance restarts the whole cycle. Turn the phone face down for the minute.
- **Treating it like a test.** If you lose count, pick it up again at the next inhale.

### If focusing on your breath feels worse

Some people find that focusing on their breath makes them more anxious. If that's you, skip the counting. Keep your eyes open, breathe normally, and just do the body steps: shoulders, jaw, gaze. If you feel dizzy, lightheaded, tingly or short of breath at any point, stop and go back to breathing normally.

This mid-scroll moment is exactly what DeRot is built for. It pauses your scroll after the feed has wound you up and walks you through a 60-second breath, so your shoulders drop and the wired feeling fades before you carry on. DeRot is coming soon to iOS.

## What the research supports, and where it's still early

There's strong evidence that slow breathing raises vagally mediated heart rate variability. Whether a longer exhale beats an even breath is less clear, and the body cues in the script (shoulders, jaw, gaze) haven't been tested. They're simply easy ways to let go of tension.

Heart rate variability (HRV) is the natural beat-to-beat variation in your heart rate. Some HRV measures, such as RMSSD and high-frequency HRV, reflect activity of the vagus nerve, the main parasympathetic "settling" pathway.

Here is what the studies show:

- **Slow breathing and HRV.** [A meta-analysis of 223 studies found slow breathing increased vagally mediated HRV during a session, immediately after a single session, and after multi-session practice](https://pure.solent.ac.uk/en/publications/effects-of-voluntary-slow-breathing-on-heart-rate-and-heart-rate-/).
- **Six breaths per minute.** [Slow breathing at six cycles per minute raised RMSSD from before to after practice, with or without HRV biofeedback](https://eprints.bournemouth.ac.uk/38163/7/Psychophysiology%20-%202021%20-%20Laborde%20-%20Psychophysiological%20effects%20of%20slow%E2%80%90paced%20breathing%20at%20six%20cycles%20per%20minute%20with%20or.pdf). The one-minute version above is shorter than the sessions typically studied. Treat it as a quick reset, and take a few minutes when you can.
- **Longer exhale.** In [a study of 28 adults, breathing out longer than breathing in, at the same overall rate, acutely increased RMSSD and high-frequency HRV, and high-frequency HRV stayed elevated for about 4 minutes afterward](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34289128/). That's encouraging, but it's one small study, and researchers haven't settled whether exhale length matters as much as simply slowing down. Use 4-6 because it's comfortable, not because it's proven to be better.
- **Mood without HRV change.** In [a month-long randomized trial, 5 minutes a day of cyclic sighing improved mood and lowered breathing rate more than mindfulness meditation](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9873947). According to a summary of the trial, [there was no significant change in HRV, and most of the 108 participants were Stanford undergraduates](https://www.simplypsychology.org/news/breathwork-practices-for-reducing-anxiety), so the results may not apply to everyone. It's also a useful reminder that feeling better and moving an HRV number aren't the same thing.

| Claim | Evidence strength | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Slow breathing raises vagally mediated HRV | Strong: meta-analysis of 223 studies | [Laborde 2022](https://pure.solent.ac.uk/en/publications/effects-of-voluntary-slow-breathing-on-heart-rate-and-heart-rate-/) |
| Six breaths per minute raises RMSSD, with or without biofeedback | Moderate: one lab study, before-and-after change | [Laborde 2021](https://eprints.bournemouth.ac.uk/38163/7/Psychophysiology%20-%202021%20-%20Laborde%20-%20Psychophysiological%20effects%20of%20slow%E2%80%90paced%20breathing%20at%20six%20cycles%20per%20minute%20with%20or.pdf) |
| A longer exhale adds extra benefit | Early and mixed: small studies | [Bae 2021](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34289128/) |
| Daily breathwork improves mood | Promising: one month-long trial, mostly students | [Balban 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9873947) |
| Scrolling raises arousal and stopping spikes stress | Early: one lab study of 54 | [Wadsley and Ihssen (Durham)](https://durham-repository.worktribe.com/OutputFile/3489734) |
| Phone posture changes breathing | Thin: 50 people, one measure differed | [Jung 2016](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4756000/) |
| Dropping shoulders, unclenching jaw, widening gaze | Untested: simple comfort cues | None |

None of this turns a breathing exercise into medical care for anxiety or any other condition. Slow breathing is associated with higher vagal HRV, and it may help you feel calmer in the moment. That's a worthwhile, modest claim, and we'd rather make that one honestly than a bigger one we can't back up.

## Regulate, don't restrict: staying connected without the overstimulation tax

"Regulate, don't restrict" means dealing with the state your phone leaves you in instead of deleting apps or shutting yourself out. You can keep the group chat, the news and the funny videos, and still stop paying the overstimulation tax.

Two moves have the best support:

- **Batch your notifications** into a few set times a day instead of switching everything off. In the 237-person experiment above, three batches a day beat both constant alerts and none at all. On an iPhone, go to Settings > Notifications > Scheduled Summary, switch it on, choose which apps to include, and set two or three delivery times. Calls, messages from people and time-sensitive alerts can still come through right away.
- **Take a breathable pause** when you notice you're wired. Run the 60-second script mid-scroll, then decide whether to keep going.

If you'd like other options, the [physiological sigh](/tools/physiological-sigh/) (two inhales through the nose, then a long, slow exhale) and [box breathing](/tools/box-breathing-timer/) are both worth trying. A safety note: breath holds and more forceful patterns, including box breathing, 4-7-8 and the physiological sigh, aren't for everyone. Take care if you're pregnant, have a heart or lung condition, or have a history of fainting or panic. Gentle 4-6 breathing, or ordinary breathing with soft shoulders, is a fine place to stay.

### When to talk to a professional

A breathing reset is for everyday overstimulation, and it doesn't replace care. If jaw clenching, headaches or neck pain keep coming back, see a dentist, doctor or physiotherapist. If anxiety, sleep problems or distress persist, talk to a professional. If you're in crisis, contact local emergency services, or call or text 988 in the US.

For everyone else, the point is a small one: you don't have to give up the feed to stop leaving it frazzled. Notice the state, come down a notch, and carry on.

## FAQ
**Why do I feel wired but tired after being on my phone?**
In a small Durham lab study, scrolling Instagram lowered heart rate while raising skin conductance, a marker of arousal. So your body may be physically still and quietly switched on at the same moment, which can feel like being wired and flat at once. Fast topic switching and emotionally charged posts probably add to it. It's one study, but it fits what a lot of people describe.

**Why do I feel anxious or irritable when I put my phone down?**
In the same Durham study of 54 young adults, heart rate and skin conductance rose after people stopped using Instagram, and they reported stress, anxiety and craving. This happened regardless of their problematic-use scores. The researchers say it's unclear whether this is withdrawal. Practically, the moment you put the phone down is a good time for a few slow breaths.

**Is it bad to turn off all notifications?**
Not necessarily bad, but it isn't always better. In a 237-person field experiment, people who got notifications in three batches a day reported better mood and lower stress, while people who got no notifications at all reported more anxiety and fear of missing out. A few predictable check-in times seem to work better than an all-or-nothing approach.

**How long does slow breathing take to calm you down?**
A meta-analysis of 223 studies found slow breathing raises vagally mediated heart rate variability during a session and right after a single one. The research doesn't set a minimum time, and a single minute is shorter than the sessions typically studied. Six breaths of 4 counts in and 6 out takes exactly 60 seconds, which makes it a practical quick reset mid-scroll. When you have more time, a few minutes is closer to what researchers test.

**Why do I clench my jaw when I'm on my phone?**
Lots of people notice that they clench their jaw, raise their shoulders or hold their breath while they're absorbed in a screen, especially when the content is tense. There's little direct research on why. A simple fix is to check in mid-scroll: part your back teeth slightly and drop your shoulders. If jaw pain or headaches keep coming back, see a dentist or doctor.

**Is doomscrolling bad for anxiety?**
A survey of 800 university students in Iran and the US found that doomscrolling was associated with higher existential anxiety. Because it was a survey taken at a single point in time, it can't show that doomscrolling causes anxiety. Anxious people may also scroll more. If bleak content leaves you rattled, choosing what you look at and taking a breathing pause mid-scroll can both help.

- Effects of voluntary slow breathing on heart rate and heart rate variability (repository listing): https://pure.solent.ac.uk/en/publications/effects-of-voluntary-slow-breathing-on-heart-rate-and-heart-rate-/

# Is Scrolling Before Bed Bad? What Matters More Than Blue Light

URL: https://derot.org/blog/is-scrolling-before-bed-bad/
Updated: 2026-10-14

Key takeaways:
- Scrolling before bed isn't automatically bad: a 2024 panel of 16 experts agreed that screens harm sleep in children and teens, but reached no consensus for adults.
- Phone light can lower melatonin, but at typical phone brightness the effect is usually modest, and sensitivity to evening light varies more than 50-fold between people.
- Night Shift made no measurable difference to sleep in a 2021 study of 167 adults aged 18 to 24.
- For many adults the bigger costs are a later bedtime and content that leaves them wired. Each extra hour of screen use in bed was linked to about 24 fewer minutes of sleep.
- How you feel when you put the phone down, drowsy or wired, tells you more about your sleep than your screen-time number does.

Scrolling before bed isn't automatically bad for sleep. For most adults, the blue light from a phone is probably a smaller factor than the headlines suggest. What tends to matter more is how much later the "one more" loop pushes your bedtime, and how wound up you feel when you finally put the phone down.

Most advice skips that last part. Two people can scroll for the same 30 minutes and have very different nights. One drifts off. The other lies there with a busy head and a tight jaw. The minutes matter less than the state you're in when you stop.

## Is scrolling before bed bad? What the experts actually agree on

Researchers agree about children and teenagers, and they don't agree about adults. In 2024, [a panel of 16 experts reviewed more than 2,200 articles on screens and sleep](https://www.colorado.edu/today/2024/05/28/light-or-content-what-we-know-about-screens-and-sleep-disruption) and reached consensus that screens and the content on them impair sleep in children and adolescents. They did not reach consensus on whether screen light impairs sleep for anyone, or on whether screen time, light or content affects adults.

That's worth sitting with, given how confidently most articles open with "yes, it's bad."

One of the largest recent studies of young adults points somewhere more specific. In [a 2025 study of 45,202 students aged 18 to 28](https://www.frontiersin.org/news/2025/03/31/hours-screen-use-after-bed-increases-insomnia-risk-frontiers-psychiatry), each extra hour of screen use after going to bed was linked to 59% higher odds of insomnia symptoms and about 24 fewer minutes of sleep. Social media was no worse than other things people did on screens in bed. Total time in bed with a screen mattered more than the app.

That study is cross-sectional, a single snapshot, so it can't show which way the arrow points. Still, it nudges the useful question away from "is my phone bad for me?" and toward "what is my scroll doing to me tonight?"

## Three ways a bedtime scroll can affect sleep

A bedtime scroll can affect your sleep in three different ways: through the light from the screen, by pushing your bedtime later, or by leaving your mind and body activated. Each has its own evidence, and most articles blend them together. Pulling them apart tells you which one, if any, applies to you.

| Mechanism | What it does | Evidence in adults | What helps |
|---|---|---|---|
| Light | Screen light can suppress melatonin and nudge your body clock later | Real in lab studies, usually modest at normal phone brightness; sensitivity varies a lot | Lower brightness, dim room lights; night mode helps only a little |
| Bedtime displacement | "One more" pushes sleep later, so you get less of it | Consistent links with shorter sleep, mostly from snapshot surveys | A rough stop time; phone charging across the room |
| Arousal | Charged content keeps your mind busy and your body activated | Plausible and expert-backed, but no formal consensus | Gentler content; a slow-exhale breath before you settle |

## Does blue light from your phone really suppress melatonin?

Yes, bright evening light, including screen light, can suppress melatonin, the hormone that rises in the evening as your body gets ready for sleep. The real question is how much a phone at ordinary brightness does, and for most adults the answer seems to be "some, but less than you've heard."

The study behind many headlines is [a 2015 lab experiment in which 12 adults read on a light-emitting eReader for four hours a night, five nights in a row](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25535358/). Compared with reading a printed book, melatonin was suppressed by 55%, its evening rise came more than 1.5 hours later, and falling asleep took about 10 minutes longer (25.7 versus 15.8 minutes). Those are real effects. They also came from four hours of reading in a dim lab, night after night, which isn't how most people use a phone.

A closer match to everyday life: [a 2024 study found that 90 minutes of reading on a smartphone lowered melatonin, but whole-night sleep was largely unaffected](https://academic.oup.com/braincomms/article/6/3/fcae173/7675955). The adults in that study had a little less deep sleep early in the night, and that was about it. It included only males aged 14 to 25, so it doesn't settle the question for everyone.

Brightness is part of the story. Stanford sleep researcher Jamie Zeitzer [estimates that a phone at night gives off roughly 25 to 50 lux, compared with 10,000 to 100,000 lux from sunlight](https://lifestylemedicine.stanford.edu/screen-time-and-sleep-its-different-for-adults).

### Why "it's probably fine" isn't the whole answer

People differ a lot in how sensitive they are to evening light. In [a 2019 study of 55 adults](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6575863), melatonin was half-suppressed at about 25 lux on average, but individual sensitivity ranged from 6 to 350 lux, a more than 50-fold difference. That study used room lighting, not phones, so it doesn't translate directly. What it does show is that an "average" effect hides a wide spread. Screen light may barely register for one person and matter more for another.

So blue light isn't nothing. For most adults it's just unlikely to be the main event.

## Does night mode or Night Shift help you sleep?

Night mode probably does little for sleep on its own. In [a 2021 BYU study of 167 adults aged 18 to 24](https://sleepreviewmag.com/sleep-treatments/therapy-devices/emerging-technology/apples-night-shift-help-sleep/), sleep did not differ between people who used their phone with Night Shift on, with Night Shift off, or who didn't use a phone at all in the hour before bed. The [BYU researchers pointed to psychological stimulation](https://magazine.byu.edu/article/good-night-night-mode) as a separate factor, one a warmer tint can't touch.

A [small University of Salzburg pilot of 14 people](https://www.plus.ac.at/news/impact-of-evening-smartphone-use/?lang=en) found that blue-light filters only partly softened the effects of evening smartphone light.

The verdict: if you like the warmer screen, leave night mode on. It's harmless. Just don't count on it to fix a bad night. The same goes for blue-light glasses: none of the studies here tested them, and we wouldn't spend money expecting them to change your sleep. If you suspect you're light-sensitive, turning the brightness down and keeping room lights low is simpler.

## The bigger factor: "one more" and a later bedtime

For many people, the main cost of a bedtime scroll is time. You pick up the phone at 10:40 to check one thing, and the next time you look at the clock it's 11:55. In [the 2025 student study](https://www.frontiersin.org/news/2025/03/31/hours-screen-use-after-bed-increases-insomnia-risk-frontiers-psychiatry), each extra hour of screen use after going to bed went with about 24 fewer minutes of sleep.

Researchers call this bedtime procrastination: putting off sleep without a real reason to stay up. In [a 2024 study of 245 adolescents](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11059092/), bedtime procrastination helped explain the link between problematic phone use and poor sleep quality. That study was of teenagers and was cross-sectional, so treat it as a plausible mechanism for adults rather than proof.

There's also a direction problem. Snapshot studies measure everything at once, so poor sleepers may reach for the phone because they can't sleep, not only the other way around. If you've ever lain awake and picked up your phone out of restlessness, you know that loop from the inside.

## Why some content leaves you wired

What you scroll may matter more than the light it's shown on. Zeitzer [argues that emotionally activating content probably matters more than screen light](https://lifestylemedicine.stanford.edu/screen-time-and-sleep-its-different-for-adults). Some people use soothing videos to wind down, though he cautions that even positive content can be stimulating. [Sleep experts at Singapore General Hospital](https://www.sgh.com.sg/news/patient-care/is-your-phone-keeping-you-awake-4-tips-for-sleep-deprived-sporeans) make a similar point: how long you use the phone near bedtime and how emotionally stimulating the content is matter more in delaying sleep.

Think about what a typical feed serves up in five minutes: a friend's baby photo, a heated argument in the comments, a work message, a news alert, a clip that makes you laugh out loud. Each one asks your nervous system to respond. Your heart runs a little quicker, your jaw sets, your thoughts start replaying the reply you didn't write. That's arousal in the physiological sense, and it's close to the opposite of the slow, heavy settling that sleep needs.

To be honest about the evidence: this explanation is plausible and backed by experts, but the 2024 panel [found no consensus on content and adult sleep either](https://www.colorado.edu/today/2024/05/28/light-or-content-what-we-know-about-screens-and-sleep-disruption). Treat it as a strong hunch you can test against your own nights. For more on this pattern, see [why doomscrolling at night leaves you wired](/blog/doomscrolling-at-night/).

## Why you fall asleep fine some nights and lie awake on others

Sleep pressure explains a lot of it. The longer you've been awake and the more tired you are, the stronger your drive to sleep. BYU researcher Chad Jensen [summed it up this way: when you're very tired, you fall asleep regardless](https://sleepreviewmag.com/sleep-treatments/therapy-devices/emerging-technology/apples-night-shift-help-sleep/) of what you did on your phone.

So after a long, draining day, a 30-minute scroll may cost you almost nothing. On a night when you're less tired, or when the feed served up something that got under your skin, the same habit can leave you staring at the ceiling.

Two other things move from night to night. Your sensitivity to light is your own ([and it varies widely between people](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6575863)), and what you happened to see changes every time you open the app. Inconsistent nights don't mean you're doing something wrong. They mean the scroll is one input among several.

## The drowsy-or-wired test

The most useful data point is how you feel in the moment you put the phone down. Next time, before you roll over, take ten seconds and notice:

- **Eyelids:** heavy, or wide open?
- **Jaw and shoulders:** soft, or held?
- **Thoughts:** drifting, or replaying something you read?
- **Heart:** slow and unremarkable, or a little quick?

**If you're drowsy,** the scroll is probably harmless, or its main cost is time. If you're waking up short on sleep, the thing to change is when you stop, not whether you scroll. Try a rough stop time for a week and see whether you wake up better rested.

**If you're wired,** arousal is the likely issue, and night mode won't touch it. What helps is changing what you look at in the last stretch (some people do fine with familiar, low-stakes content), stopping earlier, or bringing your body down before you try to sleep. If what you watch leaves you distressed or excited, Zeitzer suggests [putting the phone down about an hour before bed](https://lifestylemedicine.stanford.edu/screen-time-and-sleep-its-different-for-adults). That's expert advice rather than a tested cutoff, so treat it as a starting point you can adjust.

Run the check for a week. Many people find a pattern quickly: one app, one topic, or one kind of late-night thread that reliably leaves them buzzing, while other scrolling barely registers.

## If you're wired: a slow-exhale breath to come down

A slow breath with a longer exhale is a simple way to come down from a wired scroll. Calm 4-6 breathing means breathing in for a count of 4 and out for a count of 6, which works out to about six breaths per minute. One minute is six breaths.

1. Put the phone face down on the nightstand.
2. Breathe in gently through your nose for a count of 4, letting your belly rise.
3. Breathe out slowly through your nose or softly parted lips for a count of 6.
4. Repeat for about 60 seconds, roughly six breaths.
5. Check again: jaw, shoulders, thoughts. Notice whether anything has softened.

If counting in the dark is annoying, the [calm 4-6 breathing timer](/tools/calm-breathing-4-6/) paces it for you. For more detail on technique and common mistakes, see [how to do 4-6 breathing in 60 seconds](/blog/4-6-breathing-how-to/).

### What the evidence does and doesn't show

The most relevant trial is encouraging. In [a 2019 randomized trial with 64 participants analyzed](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6406675/), 15 minutes of slow breathing at about six breaths per minute each evening for 30 days improved self-reported sleep quality and overnight vagal activity (a marker of the nervous system's calming branch). A comparison group that spent the same 15 minutes on social media saw no change. That was 15 minutes a night for a month, though. A 60-second version is less tested.

A [2020 pilot of 20 young adults](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7198497/) found that 30 minutes of slow breathing before bed raised heart rate variability right away but had no robust effect on sleep measured in the lab. The honest summary: slow breathing can help you feel calmer in the moment, which may make settling easier. It isn't a sleep treatment.

That mid-scroll moment, when you notice you're wound up but still holding the phone, is what DeRot is being built for. It meets you mid-scroll and walks you through a minute of breathing, so you put the phone down with your shoulders lower and your head quieter. It's coming soon to iOS. For a fuller wind-down routine, see the [night doomscrolling guide](/blog/doomscrolling-at-night/), and browse more in [sleep and winding down](/blog/topics/sleep-and-winding-down/).

### A few safety notes

Keep the breathing gentle. If you feel dizzy or lightheaded, stop and breathe normally. The 4-6 pattern has no breath holds, but if you're pregnant, have a heart or lung condition, or have a history of fainting or panic, skip breath holds and fast breathing and check with your doctor before trying new techniques.

Changing your phone habits or your breathing won't treat insomnia. If poor sleep happens most nights for several weeks, or it's affecting your days, talk to a doctor or sleep specialist. If the wired feeling is really recurring anxiety or distress, a professional can help. If you might be in crisis, contact local emergency services, or call or text 988 in the US.

## FAQ
**Is social media worse than watching TV or reading on my phone before bed?**
Not necessarily. In a 2025 study of 45,202 students aged 18 to 28, social media was no worse for sleep than other screen activities in bed. Total time on screens after going to bed mattered more. What you see still counts, though: a heated comment thread can leave you more activated than a familiar show. How you feel when you stop is a better guide than the app's name.

**How long before bed should I stop using my phone?**
There's no tested cutoff. If what you watch leaves you distressed or excited, Stanford sleep researcher Jamie Zeitzer suggests stopping about an hour before bed, but that's expert advice rather than a rule from the studies here. A practical approach is to notice how you feel when you put the phone down. If you're drowsy and sleeping enough, your current habit may be fine. If you're wired or regularly losing sleep, try stopping earlier or switching to calmer content.

**Do blue-light glasses help with sleep?**
There isn't good evidence that they do, and none of the research reviewed for this article tested them. Related studies suggest blue-light filters only partly soften the effects of evening phone light, and Night Shift made no measurable difference to sleep in a 2021 study of young adults. Lowering screen brightness and keeping room lights dim is simpler and costs nothing.

**Is it okay to watch calming videos to fall asleep?**
For some people, yes. Stanford sleep researcher Jamie Zeitzer has said emotionally activating content probably matters more than screen light, though he cautions that even positive content can be stimulating. If a quiet, familiar video leaves you drowsy, it's likely fine. If you keep queuing up one more and bedtime keeps slipping later, the cost is lost sleep time.

**What should I do if I feel wired after scrolling in bed?**
Put the phone face down and try a minute of slow breathing with a longer exhale, such as breathing in for 4 counts and out for 6. It can help you feel calmer in the moment, though it isn't a sleep treatment. Stop if you feel lightheaded. If feeling wired at night is a regular pattern tied to anxiety or distress, talk to a professional.

# 4-6 Breathing: How to Do the Calm Pattern in 60 Seconds

URL: https://derot.org/blog/4-6-breathing-how-to/
Updated: 2026-10-12

Key takeaways:
- 4-6 breathing means breathing in through the nose for 4 counts and out for 6, with no holds, which works out to about 10 seconds per breath and about 6 breaths per minute.
- Six slow breaths take roughly one minute, so 4-6 breathing fits neatly into a mid-scroll pause when you notice a clenched jaw or a wired feeling.
- Most mistakes come from trying too hard: gulping the inhale, pushing the exhale, counting too fast, or holding at the top out of habit.
- If a 6-count exhale feels too long, keep the shape and shorten the counts to 3-5. Comfort matters more than hitting exact numbers.
- Research most clearly supports the slow pace itself; a longer exhale may add to how relaxed you feel, but it hasn't shown a clear extra benefit over equal breathing.

4-6 breathing is a slow breathing pattern in which you breathe in through your nose for 4 counts and out for 6, with no breath holds. Each breath takes about 10 seconds, so you breathe about 6 times a minute. Six breaths is roughly one minute, which makes it an easy reset right in the middle of a scroll.

It's the pattern to reach for when you surface from a feed with your shoulders up and your head buzzing: nothing to hold, nothing complicated to count, just a slightly longer out-breath than in-breath.

## What is 4-6 breathing?

4-6 breathing (sometimes written 4:6, or called extended exhale breathing) is a no-hold pattern: in for a count of 4, out for a count of 6, then straight into the next breath. At roughly one count per second, a full breath takes 10 seconds and the pace lands at about 6 breaths per minute.

That pace is the useful part. Six breaths take about a minute, which fits into the gap between noticing you're wound up and deciding what to do next. A UK mental health guide, [Breathing Out Anxiety](https://www.theppt.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/Breathing-Out-Anxiety.pdf), recommends exactly this pattern: in for 4, out for 6, without holding your breath.

A few similar names cause confusion:

- **4-4-6 and 4-2-6** keep the longer out-breath but add a hold of 4 or 2 counts after the inhale. That slows the pace further and gives you one more thing to count.
- **Coherent or resonance breathing** (often 5-5) runs at about the same pace, roughly 6 breaths a minute, but the in-breath and out-breath are equal.
- **4-7-8** is a different pattern entirely, built around a long 7-count hold.

If you'd rather not count in your head, the [free calm 4-6 breathing timer](/tools/calm-breathing-4-6/) paces each breath for you.

## How to do 4-6 breathing, step by step

To do 4-6 breathing, breathe in gently through your nose for 4 counts, then breathe out slowly for 6 counts with no pause in between, and repeat for 6 breaths. Here is the full version:

1. **Get settled.** Sit or stand with your shoulders loose and your hands resting. Sit while you're learning, in case you feel lightheaded.
2. **Breathe in softly through your nose for 4.** Fill to about 70-80% of a full breath, not to the brim. Let your belly and lower ribs widen rather than lifting your shoulders.
3. **With no pause at the top, breathe out slowly for 6.** Use your nose or softly pursed lips, as if cooling a spoonful of soup. Let the air leave; don't squeeze it out.
4. **Let the next inhale start on its own.** There may be a tiny natural turnaround at the bottom. Don't turn it into a hold.
5. **Repeat for 6 breaths.** That's about one minute.

Count at roughly one per second. "One-and, two-and" is a reliable way to stop the count from speeding up.

### Nose or mouth?

Breathe in through your nose; it's quieter and makes a slow inhale easier to control. Breathe out through either. Pursed lips make it easier to stretch the exhale to 6, while breathing out through the nose is less noticeable on a train or in an office.

## A 60-second 4-6 breathing script for mid-scroll

The best moment for 4-6 breathing is partway through the feed, when you notice your jaw is set, your shoulders have crept up, or you feel a hum of irritation or a slightly sped-up, wired feeling. You don't have to close the app or decide anything yet. Put the phone face down on your knee, or just look away from the screen.

**Breath 1 (0-10 seconds).** In, 2, 3, 4. Out, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Just slow down. If the count wobbles, let it. No judging.

**Breaths 2-3 (10-30 seconds).** Keep the same count. On each out-breath, let your shoulders drop a little. Don't place them; let them fall.

**Breaths 4-5 (30-50 seconds).** On the out-breath, unclench your jaw: teeth slightly apart, tongue resting. Soften your eyes and let your gaze widen to the room.

**Breath 6 (50-60 seconds).** Notice what changed, even if it's small. Then decide on purpose: go back to the feed, answer the message, or put the phone down.

The goal here is your state, not your screen time. You're not trying to log off or earn a streak. If you go back to scrolling a notch calmer, that counts. (If this happens to you mostly in bed, our guide to [doomscrolling at night](/blog/doomscrolling-at-night/) covers that moment specifically.)

This mid-scroll minute is what DeRot is built around. It pauses your scroll after the feed has wound you up and walks you through a minute of Calm breathing (in 4, out 6), so your shoulders drop and the wired feeling fades before you carry on. It's coming soon to iOS; until then, the free timer does the counting.

## What 4-6 breathing feels like (and what it shouldn't)

Done comfortably, 4-6 breathing usually feels like a gradual settling: your breath gets quieter, your shoulders come down, your jaw loosens and the buzzy edge eases over a minute or so. These are common experiences, not guarantees. Some days you'll notice a lot, some days very little, and both are normal.

It shouldn't feel like a strain. Watch for:

- **Air hunger**, the sense that you're not getting enough air
- **Gasping** or grabbing at the next inhale
- **Tingling** in your fingers or lips
- **Lightheadedness** or chest discomfort

Any of these means the counts are too long or the breaths too big. Shorten to 3-5, or stop and breathe normally.

## Common 4-6 breathing mistakes

Most 4-6 breathing mistakes come from trying too hard. The pattern works best when it feels slightly lazy.

- **Gulping the inhale.** Filling to the brim in 4 counts makes the breath sharp. Sip in to about 70-80% instead.
- **Pushing the exhale.** Forcing the air out tenses your belly and throat. Let the breath leave slowly, like a tyre with a slow leak.
- **Counting too fast.** If your 4-and-6 takes 6 seconds instead of 10, you're at about 10 breaths a minute, right at the cutoff of what researchers [define as slow breathing](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30245619/) (fewer than 10 a minute). Check against a timer once to calibrate.
- **Lifting the shoulders.** Chest-and-shoulder breathing works against the point. Let the belly and lower ribs do the moving.
- **Holding at the top out of habit.** If you usually do box or 4-7-8, you may pause automatically. Turn straight from in to out.
- **Big open-mouth sighs.** One sigh is fine. Several deep, fast ones in a row can tip you into over-breathing, which is often what causes tingling.
- **Getting perfectionist about the count.** If counting makes you tense, drop the numbers. Just make each out-breath a little longer than the in-breath.

## What if 6 seconds feels too long? Try 3-5 first

If a 6-count exhale leaves you short of air, keep the shape and shorten the counts: in for 3, out for 5. That's 8 seconds per breath, or about 7 to 8 breaths a minute, which is still slow breathing.

A gentle progression looks like this:

1. **3-5** until it feels easy
2. **4-6**, the standard pattern
3. **5-7** (about 5 breaths a minute), optional, only if 4-6 starts to feel effortless

You can set any of these on the [custom breathing timer](/tools/custom-breathing-timer/). Comfort beats hitting exact numbers. A relaxed 3-5 does more for you than a strained 4-6.

## 4-6 breathing vs 4-7-8 vs box breathing: which is gentler?

For most people, 4-6 breathing is the gentlest of the common patterns because it has no breath holds. There's nothing to hold through and only two numbers to track, which suits people who find holds uncomfortable or who get a little panicky when air is "stopped."

The table below is our practical guide, not study data: the breaths-per-minute figures are simple arithmetic at one count per second, and the difficulty and dizziness ratings reflect how these patterns tend to feel.

| Pattern | Holds | Breaths per minute (approx.) | Difficulty | Dizziness risk | Best moment |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4-6 (calm) | None | 6 | Easy | Low, if the inhale stays soft | Mid-scroll, any time you feel wound up |
| Box (4-4-4-4) | Two 4-count holds | 3.75 | Moderate | Low to moderate | When you want something structured to focus on |
| 4-7-8 | One 7-count hold | About 3 | Harder | Moderate | Winding down, sitting or lying |
| Physiological sigh | None (double inhale, long exhale) | Varies | Easy | Low for a few breaths; higher if rushed | A quick reset of one to a few breaths |

Holds aren't bad, and other patterns have real support. NHS inform's [controlled breathing exercise](https://www.nhsinform.scot/healthy-living/mental-wellbeing/breathing-and-relaxation-exercises/controlled-breathing-exercise) uses a 3-3-3-3 pattern with holds. A 2023 study in Cell Reports Medicine found that [daily 5-minute cyclic sighing improved mood and lowered respiratory rate more than mindfulness meditation](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9873947) over one month.

If you want to compare them yourself, try the [box breathing timer](/tools/box-breathing-timer/), the [4-7-8 breathing timer](/tools/4-7-8-breathing-timer/) or the [physiological sigh guide](/tools/physiological-sigh/).

## Why does a longer exhale help? A short, honest summary

The honest answer is that the slow pace seems to do most of the work. A longer exhale may add to how relaxed you feel, but it hasn't shown a clear extra benefit over equal in and out breaths.

The case for slow breathing is fairly solid. A review of 15 studies found that [breathing at under 10 breaths a minute was associated with higher heart rate variability (HRV) and more comfort and relaxation](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30245619/), though the evidence base was small. A larger meta-analysis of 223 studies found that [vagally mediated HRV rose during slow breathing, right after a single session, and after multi-session practice](https://eprints.bournemouth.ac.uk/38169/).

The exhale ratio is more mixed:

- In a study of 30 people, [a long exhale produced more self-reported relaxation and less stress than a long inhale](https://research.vu.nl/en/publications/inhalationexhalation-ratio-modulates-the-effect-of-slow-breathing/), with an HRV gain that appeared only at 6 breaths a minute.
- In a randomised trial with 94 adults analysed, [anxiety fell in both the longer-exhale and equal-breathing groups, with no significant difference between them](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10395759/).
- A comparison of 1:1 and 1:2 breathing at 6 breaths a minute (26 people, plus a replication with 16) found [no difference in HRV](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11310264/).
- One study even found an [HRV advantage for equal breathing at 5.5 breaths a minute](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24380741/).

The usual explanation involves the vagus nerve and the rest-and-digest side of the nervous system. It's plausible and partly supported, but not settled. Practically: slow down first, and use the longer exhale because it feels good, not because it's magic.

## How long should you do 4-6 breathing?

One minute, or six breaths, is enough for a mid-scroll reset. It's short enough to actually do and long enough to notice a shift.

If you want a longer practice, the NHS suggests [repeating calming breathing for at least 5 minutes](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/stress-anxiety-depression/ways-relieve-stress/) and notes it can be done anywhere, and the PPT guide suggests [building up gradually to 10 minutes](https://www.theppt.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/Breathing-Out-Anxiety.pdf).

Keep expectations proportional. A meta-analysis of breathwork trials found a [small-to-medium reduction in stress (12 RCTs, 785 adults)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9828383/), with most studies at moderate risk of bias. That's encouraging, and still developing.

## A quick safety note

4-6 breathing is gentle, but stop and go back to normal breathing if you feel dizzy, lightheaded, tingly or short of air, or have any chest discomfort. Sit or lie down while you're learning. If you're pregnant, have a heart or lung condition, or have a history of fainting or panic attacks, check with a clinician before making any breathing practice a regular habit.

Breathing can help you feel calmer and may reduce stress, but it doesn't treat anxiety, panic or insomnia. If anxiety, distress or sleep problems keep coming back, talk to a professional. If you're in crisis, call 988 in the US or your local emergency services.

## FAQ
**Is 4-6 breathing the same as 4-7-8?**
No. 4-6 breathing is in for 4 and out for 6 with no holds, at about 6 breaths a minute. 4-7-8 is in for 4, hold for 7, out for 8, which works out to about 3 breaths a minute. The long hold makes 4-7-8 harder for many people and more likely to cause lightheadedness, so 4-6 is usually the easier one to start with or to use mid-scroll.

**Is 4-6 breathing the same as coherent or resonance breathing?**
They're close relatives. Coherent or resonance breathing is usually done at about 6 breaths a minute with equal in and out breaths, such as 5-5. 4-6 breathing has the same pace but a longer exhale. Studies comparing equal and longer-exhale breathing at this pace have found no clear heart rate variability advantage for the longer exhale, and one small study favoured equal breathing, so pick whichever feels more comfortable.

**Why do I feel dizzy or short of air doing 4-6 breathing?**
Usually the breaths are too big or the counts are too long for you right now. Gulping a full inhale or pushing out a long exhale can tip you into over-breathing or air hunger. Stop and breathe normally, then try again with softer breaths at about 70-80% of a full breath, or shorten the counts to 3-5. If dizziness keeps happening, check with a doctor.

**Can 4-6 breathing help me fall asleep?**
It may help you feel calmer as you wind down, which some people find makes it easier to drift off. Try a few minutes lying down with soft breaths and no pressure to count perfectly. It isn't a treatment for insomnia, though. If you regularly struggle to fall or stay asleep, talk to a doctor or sleep professional.

**What's the difference between 4-6 and 4-4-6 or 4-2-6 breathing?**
All three use a longer out-breath, but 4-4-6 adds a 4-count hold after the inhale and 4-2-6 adds a 2-count hold. The holds slow the pace further and add a step to track. 4-6 has no holds at all, so it's the simplest version and the one to choose if holding your breath feels uncomfortable.

- Breathing at 5.5 breaths per minute with equal inhalation-to-exhalation ratio increases HRV (Lin et al.): https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24380741/
